en: Satisfying the two saintly Śrīla Rūpa and Sanātana,
this work is now analyzed by the southern Bhaṭṭa, Pṛthu. Om.
Having thoroughly examined the first manuscript of that work— which was displaced, missing, and fragmentary—
and having made a systematic arrangement, Jīvaka writes it down. [1] Now, the composition of the *Prīti-sandarbha* is to be written.
Indeed, the supreme reality to be established by this treatise has previously been connected through four sections;
and the worship of that [reality] follows immediately thereafter.
It has been stated by way of context;
now, indeed, the purpose is being analyzed according to its sequential order.
The purpose of the person (puruṣārtha) consists, first of all, in the attainment of happiness and the cessation of suffering;
however, in the case of pleasing the Blessed Lord, the nature of happiness and the cessation of suffering are both absolute.

This is what is meant: that which was previously determined as the supreme reality (parama-tattva) to be propounded by the scriptures is established precisely as being existent, infinite, and supreme bliss.

In the Śruti as well, beginning with the words "This is the inquiry into bliss," the text demonstrates the progressive measure of the excellence of their bliss— increased tenfold and hundredfold respectively— from human bliss up to the bliss of the progenitors (prājāpatya), and then once again...
Furthermore, even after demonstrating that the bliss of the Supreme Brahman is a hundred times greater than that, [the author], being unsatisfied,
establishes by means of the verse beginning with "from which words turn back" both the infinitude and the transcendent distinctness of that bliss.
"For who indeed could breathe, who could live, if this bliss were not in the ether? By this,
it is shown that even in terms of its various forms and attributes, its essential nature is solely that of bliss,
just as the solar orb and others of such a kind possess the nature of light alone.
Furthermore, although the individual soul (jīva) belongs to Him, it is overwhelmed by His Māyā due to being characterized by the absence of contact with His knowledge; thus,
through the loss of knowledge of its own true nature and the penetration of adjuncts (upādhi) fashioned by Māyā,
it becomes bound by the suffering of beginningless saṃsāra— this is stated in the *Paramātma-sandarbha* and other works.
This has been explained;
from this it follows that the attainment of supreme bliss is precisely that knowledge characterized by the direct realization of the ultimate reality.
That alone is the supreme human goal:
the cessation of ignorance regarding one's own self and the absolute cessation of suffering. When that ignorance—the root cause—is removed, these two are accomplished spontaneously.

Because the former consists essentially of the manifestation of the self-luminosity of the supreme reality (*parama-tattva*), and because the latter is of the nature of non-existence through destruction (*dhvaṃsābhāva*), it is imperishable.
And it has been stated that dharma is the supreme human goal in such passages as, "For dharma indeed leads to liberation" (BhP 1.2.9);
therefore, the sages, possessing faith in that, endowed with knowledge and detachment—
And they perceive the Self within themselves through devotion acquired by hearing [the scriptures].

Thus, up to the end of [BhP 1.2.12], the cessation of all suffering by its own nature is stated in that very same place, beginning with: "The knot of the heart is severed" [BhP 1.2.13]. And in the Śrī Viṣṇu Purāṇa:

"The attainment of the Blessed One, characterized solely by the state of bliss consisting of unsurpassed and extraordinary delight, is considered the singular, absolute, and final medicine" (ViP 6.5.59).
And in the Śruti: "The knower of the bliss of Brahman fears nothing from anywhere" (TaittU 2.4.1).
And this alone is the meaning of the word "liberation" (mukti),
because it is preceded by the severing of the bonds of saṃsāra; as it was said by the venerable Sūta:
When, by means of this weapon of discrimination, one has thus severed the bondage of the self consisting of the ego-identification born of Māyā,
one remains established in the experience of the imperishable Self.
Regarding this, they say: "O dear one, that is the ultimate dissolution" (BhP 12.4.34).

The meaning is that when one remains established as such—possessing direct experience (*anubhava*) of the Self known as Acyuta, the Supreme Self—that is called the ultimate dissolution, which is liberation.
Furthermore, the statement that "liberation is the abiding in one's own nature after abandoning any other form" (BhP 2.10.6) has precisely the same meaning as that [previous definition],
because what is called "abiding in one's own nature" is the direct realization of one's own nature.

It is said: because that mere state [of being] persists even during the condition of saṃsāra; and because "having a different form" means merely the non-cognition of that [state], such that when that [non-cognition] is abandoned, it culminates in the cognition of that [state]. Furthermore, the "own-nature" (svarūpa) here is primarily characterized as the Supreme Self (paramātman).
For He alone is the supreme nature of the whole (aṃśin) for all living beings, just as the sun is to its rays and atoms;
as it was said to Brahmā:

"O glorious one, when he perceives himself as devoid of the elements, the senses, the qualities, and the latent impressions, and as endowed with me in my own essential nature, he attains self-sovereignty. (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 3.9.33)
"Endowed" (*upetam*) means "joined" (*yuktam*); thus, the meaning is unblemished.
It has been shown that the very nature of the individual soul (*jīva*) is secondary bliss (*gauṇānanda*). Therefore, after stating, "[The Self is] the most beloved" (BhP 10.14.54)—
"Know this Kṛṣṇa to be the Self of all selves;

for the welfare of the world, He also appears here as if possessing a body through His Māyā. By this [BhP 10.14.55], the doctrine of the non-difference between the individual soul and the Supreme is established, especially in the *Paramātma-sandarbha* and other works.
It has been avoided; therefore, the Śruti determined: "He is indeed the essence (rasa); for having obtained the essence, this one becomes blissful" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.7.1).

In this context, the attainment of the whole through its parts should be understood in two ways. Of these, the first is the attainment of Brahman, which consists merely in the manifestation of the knowledge of that [Brahman]— characterized by its own essential power— immediately following the destruction of ignorance (avidyā) as a modification of Māyā.
And that [attainment] may occur either in its own place, or it may occur after gradually transcending all worldly obscurations; this depends on the specific nature of one's practice.
The second [type] is the attainment of the Blessed One, because even though that All-pervading Lord is not manifest everywhere, He manifests Himself in that very place;
whereas the All-pervading Lord is manifest everywhere in Vaikuṇṭha.
And by that [Lord] of inconceivable power, through the attainment of proximity to his own lotus-feet;
such being the case,
that liberation occurs both in the state of transmigration (*utkrānta-daśā*) and in the state of the individual soul (*jīva-daśā*).

Because even when one has departed [from the body], despite the absence of limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), the non-interruption of the attribute characterized by its own self-luminosity constitutes the nature of this direct realization;
and while alive, it is through that direct realization [that it is known].
Because the transformation of that which is imagined through illusion appears as false, this very state is taught as liberation itself, being the ultimate human goal;
even there, liberation alone is desired as the ultimate end.
"Since the goal consisting of the three aims of life is eternally joined with the fear of *kṛtānta* (death)," thus [spoke] Śrī Sanatkumāra to Śrī Pṛthu.
And the Śruti says: "By what means might I become immortal?"
"What could I do with that? (BAU 2.4.3).
Thus, since liberation—which consists in the direct realization of the supreme reality—is established as the supreme human goal, then...
It is analyzed: and that supreme reality manifests in two ways—
as that which has indistinct particularities and as that which consists of distinct particularities that are its own essential nature.

In that regard, even when compared to the direct realization of the supreme reality characterized by distinct attributes known as Brahman, the direct realization of that same reality characterized by distinct attributes known as Bhagavān, Paramātman, and so forth, is superior; this is stated in the *Bhagavat-sandarbha* [87].
"O Lord, although that eternal Brahman has been sought after and studied,
you nevertheless grieve for yourself as if your purpose were unfulfilled"—
this and more I have demonstrated through this series of textual passages.
In this regard as well, I shall show another scriptural statement:
"Therefore, [the Lord], who possesses various states characterized by being the Supreme Self and so forth— "
In that case as well, direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*) itself is supreme.

Even though its nature consists in being the locus of untainted joy (*nirupadhi-prīti*), when there is the direct realization of the multitude of its own essential attributes (*svarūpa-dharmāntara*), [that joy] becomes supreme. Regarding this joy—
They consider the direct realization of the specific quality characterized by dearness—known as devotion (*bhakti*) and so forth—to be the supreme goal;
and through that very love, there is the cessation of ultimate suffering. That which...
Without joy (*prīti*), the direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*) of its essential nature and the multitude of its other qualities is not accomplished;
where that [joy] exists, there it is necessarily accomplished.
To whatever extent there is the perfection of joy, to that same extent is the perfection of that [object];
when it is being perfected and once it is perfected, it becomes even more so.
It manifests;
all of this is indeed logical.
For the Blessed One’s supreme bliss is indeed [supreme].
Furthermore, the nature of that multitude of qualities is bliss, which is the locus of unconditional love; therefore,
in the experience of that [bliss], love itself is primary.
Therefore, it is established that since a person must always seek that [liberation] alone, it is precisely therein that the ultimate purpose of a person resides;
this will now be illustrated in sequence.
Regarding that, the passage beginning with "Even though... states:
"By the yoga of devotion to me, my devotee attains everything directly—both heaven and liberation, as well as my own abode—if he so desires. (BhP 11.20.33)
"Thus," and so forth, refers to the words of the Blessed Lord at the beginning [of the text].
"By that," and so forth:
"As long as there is no love for me, Vāsudeva..."
"One is not liberated from the connection with the body so long [as this remains]," thus says the word of Śrī Ṛṣabhadeva;
and regarding the verse beginning with "yām" (her whom...):
"I am to be grasped by exclusive devotion and by faith; I am the Self, dear to the virtuous"—
thus it is in the word of the Blessed Lord.
Regarding the passage beginning with "sampadyamāne":
"Through devotion, one knows my form— the non-dual Brahman, devoid of middle, beginning, and end, self-luminous, existence-consciousness-bliss, and imperishable."
Thus it is said in the Vāsudevopaniṣad; regarding the passage beginning with "where," etc.,
it is devotion alone that leads one there.
Devotion alone reveals Him;
the person is under the sway of devotion, for devotion is indeed supreme.
Thus it is stated in the Māṭhara-śruti.
Regarding the passage beginning with "yāvatī" and so forth:
devotion, the experience of the Supreme Lord, and dispassion...
Moreover, this triad occurs at a single time for one who is undertaking [the practice],
just as for one who is eating, there are satisfaction, nourishment, and the removal of hunger with every morsel.
In the words of the Lord of Poets (Śrī Kṛṣṇa),
as well as in scriptural passages such as "That thou art" (tat tvam asi), it should be understood that the ultimate goal is love for Him alone, just as in the expression "You are indeed so-and-so."
Furthermore, even worldly convention is seen to be directed toward that alone; for all living beings have pleasure as their sole purpose,
since they are observed to undergo even the loss of their own lives for its sake.
However, failing to find a suitable object, that [devotion] is diverted by them elsewhere;
therefore, when everyone desires to seek yoga and its objects, it culminates in the Blessed Lord alone.
"May it be so. Thus, having established that the pleasure of the Blessed Lord alone is the supreme goal of human life (*puruṣārtha*), it was rightly said:
"Now, the composition of [this] Pleasure shall be written," and so forth.
This very same supreme goal of human life is now to be demonstrated as being at the very pinnacle of all things, according to the sequential order.
It is being woven together.

In this regard, he states that liberation in its general sense, as defined above, is the purpose of the scripture, beginning with the words "sarva-vedānta... and concluding with "...kaivalyaika-prayojanam" (BhP 12.13.12). It is *kevala* (absolute/isolated).
Purity is its state, which is isolation (*kaivalya*).
That which has this alone as its sole purpose—established as the supreme human goal—is this *Śrī-Bhāgavata*; thus [ends] the previous [section].
The syntactical connection is with the verse.
For it has been stated that the very absence of knowledge of the supreme reality is the root of the living entity’s defects—
beginning with the words "Fear arises from attachment to a second" (BhP 12.2.37)— from the Lord.
By the words "of one who has departed" and so forth,
it follows that purity is precisely the knowledge of that [Self]; thus, as before, the purport of the word *kaivalya* (isolation) here is simply the experience thereof.
Alternatively, by the word *kaivalya*, the very nature of the Supreme is expressed;
as it is said in the Skanda Purāṇa:
"That which cannot be attained even by the gods, beginning with Brahmā and Īśāna..."

"That which is His own nature is absolute isolation (kaivalya); You, O Hari, are that absolute one. In some instances, the word *kaivalya*—ending in a *taddhita* suffix used in its own sense (*svārthika*)—also denotes the Supreme, as in the *Śrī-Dattātreyopadeśa*:
"He dwells as the supreme among the high and the low, designated as Kaivalya; he is the mass of the bliss of absolute experience, free from all limiting adjuncts" (BhP 11.9.18).
Nevertheless, in both cases, the primary purport is precisely that experience of Him.
Or rather, it has that very same nature;
the meaning is that this treatise has been composed in order to experience that very [reality].
And so it is stated elsewhere:
"To this extent alone should the self-interest of men—whose intellects are skilled in yoga—be known with their whole being: that the Self of others is the very same as one's own. [BhP 6.16.63]

And the commentary (*ṭīkā*) says: "He states 'this much' (*etāvān*) to show that there is no person (*puruṣa*) beyond this. That which is the single vision of the supreme Self is expressed by the phrase 'just this much' (*etāvān eva*)."
Or, it is the vision of the absolute Supreme Self alone. Thus spoke Śrī Śaṅkarṣaṇa to Citraketu.
Indeed, this liberation occurs in two ways during the state of departure: either immediately, or... [3] ...at once.
And according to the sequential order: therein,
the first is "In the second [chapter], the seat is firm and comfortable" (BhP 2.2.15), and so forth.
At the end of the section, one should dismiss [the deity] with the words "yataḥ param" (BhP 2.2.21). And immediately following that,
in the verse beginning "yadi prayāsyan nṛpa pārameṣṭhyam" (BhP 2.2.22), one should [meditate on] the Self by means of that very Self.
Regarding the phrase "he attains peace" [BhP 2.2.31],
that [peace] should be shown first even during the state of being alive, specifically within its particular manifestations.
In that regard, he describes liberation while living (jīvan-mukti), characterized by the direct realization of Brahman:

"When both the existent and the non-existent forms have been negated here by one's own consciousness, [realizing] they were produced in the Self through ignorance—that is the vision of Brahman. [BhP 1.3.33]

In which philosophical system (darśana), by means of one's own consciousness— that is, through the knowledge of the true nature of the individual self (jīvātman)— do the gross and subtle bodies become negated?
In what manner?
In reality, those two do not exist at all in the Self; rather, they are merely superimposed upon the Self through ignorance—this is the meaning of the phrase "in this manner.
The connection between the relative pronoun *yat* and the demonstrative pronoun *tat* is as follows: "that" refers to the vision of Brahman (*brahma-darśana*).
The vision of Brahman is direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*).
By the statement "wherein there is self-cognition," the knowledge of the nature of the individual soul (*jīva*) is also understood as having that [Brahman] as its substratum.
Thus it is;

likewise, it has been made known that by means of their own pure self-awareness (*svasaṃvid*), those two do not exist when they have been negated. And therefore, even while living, [there is] the connection with the effects of illusion (*māyā*) constructed by ignorance (*avidyā*).

The meaning is that the direct realization of Brahman, attained through identity with the direct perception of the true nature of the self which reveals its own falsity, is a specific form of liberation while living (jīvanmukti).
//1.3// Śrī Sūta:
//3// [4] This very definition of liberation has been shown in the four verses beginning with "That liberation, which has its refuge in the Blessed Kapila" (BhP 3.28.35–38).
For in that state, having turned back the flow of qualities,
one beholds oneself as the Supreme Self; thus, being established in the glory that constitutes one's own true nature,
having attained the final goal, and having realized the ultimate limit of the Supreme Self, he too [attains liberation] by this very means.

In the beginning, [the text] states "the true nature of the individual soul and Brahman" (*jīva-brahmaṇo yāthātmyam*) and "having entered into the midst of the body and the objects of thought" (*madhyagamad iti dehaṃ ca*); likewise, it states "thus is the realized reality" (*evaṃ pratibuddha-vastu*) and "even the body" (*deho'pi*).
Therefore, for him—
The experience of those actions alone that have already begun (*prārabdha-karma*) occurs precisely through non-attachment;
thus it has been said therein: "What delusion, what sorrow can there be for one who perceives oneness? (Īśopaniṣad 7).

Now he describes the final liberation, characterized by the direct realization of Brahman: "If this goddess Māyā has indeed ceased, they know him as one who has truly attained perfection; thus, in his own glory, he is magnified. (BhP 1.3.34)

This radiant intellect, which is the Goddess and the very form of knowledge (vidyā), has been bestowed by the wise Supreme Lord; it abides in the state of liberation while living (jīvanmukti). If that sattvic modification of Māyā—which is characterized as the door for the manifestation of Vidya, being a function of Māyā’s own essential power (svarūpa-śakti)—should cease or withdraw, [then liberation is attained].
When that occurs, because there is an absence even of the appearance of any intervening obstruction, the sages know that one has indeed attained the perfection of the bliss of Brahman.
And consequently, from the attainment of that perfection, in oneself...
Even in its own essential perfection (*svarūpa-sampatti*), it is magnified (*mahīyate*), meaning it is worshiped;
the sense is that it becomes preeminent light (*prakṛṣṭa-prakāśa*).

// 1.3 // The Son of Śrī // 4 // [5] Here, in the preceding sections concerning Tattva, Bhagavān, and Paramātman, this has been established by means of its intrinsic value as well as through the Śrutis and other authorities. (Page 6)

Indeed, the individual soul (jīva) is a single part of the Supreme Reality, which is characterized by the collective power known as the living principle (jīvākhya-samaṣṭi-śakti). And that soul is like a moving particle of light outside a sphere of radiance; it is a moving particle of consciousness outside that [Reality], whose sole essence is supreme consciousness.

In that case, because it is all-pervasive, the soul would indeed occupy only a single part of it; however, since it is formless, occupying a single part is not contradictory. Nevertheless, its movement outside [the body] occurs by virtue of depending upon that [body].
Due to the absence of knowledge of that [Self], and because it is capable of being obscured by *māyā*— just as a ray [is obscured] by its shadow— it is designated as "moving externally.
Furthermore, it occupies the position of the ray.
Because it is distinct from that [external object], its state of being the substratum is understood through its distinctness;
and by means of the aforementioned reasoning,
as well as through such scriptural passages as "the one reality even when moving externally," this is established.
And its nature as power (*śaktitva*) is due to its being an instrument for His divine play (*līlā*) precisely by virtue of having that form;
and its atomicity (*aṇutva*) is [known] from the word "Hari-candana."
Because its power, characterized by its specific qualities, pervades the entire body like a drop of collyrium;
and all of this is not contradictory because it arises from the supreme being whose nature consists of inconceivable power, as has been firmly established previously through scripture.
According to the principle that "it is rooted in the word" (Nyāya-sūtra 2.1.17),

and by the argument beginning with "of the fire situated in one part," there would be the further impossibility of the simultaneous possession of ignorance and knowledge if there were absolute non-difference between the individual soul (jīva) and the Lord (īśvara).
The previous [explanation] has already been set forth.

However, in such cases as "That thou art" (*tattvam asi*), figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) functions identically in both the case of absolute non-difference and the case of being a part thereof. As for the scriptural teaching that the supreme reality is partless, it proceeds in two ways; therein—

The primary function [of this teaching] is solely directed toward the definition of the pure substantive (viśeṣya); for that [reality] consists of nothing but bliss. It is the definition of that which has the singular form of bliss, as distinguished by its own essential power (svarūpa-śakti).
However, the secondary application [of the term] regarding *parā* (the supreme nature) intends merely its freedom from even a trace of the *prākṛta* (material) portion;
for that [nature], which is distinguished by all powers, is indeed proclaimed to be the whole (*sarvāṃśin*).
Thus, when it is established that it possesses portions comparable to rays or atoms, the same applies to everything else as well.
In that state, even their essential attributes, such as agency and enjoyership, are established;
and likewise,
it is solely through the grace of the Supreme Lord’s power that they become capable of performing their functions therein.
The state of being an agent consisting of primordial nature (prakṛti) and its transformations, and so forth, occurs through the grace of His illusory power (māyā-śakti).
Therefore, due to that connection, they undergo saṃsāra;
[this ends] with their own experience and the experience of Brahman.
However, the Lord’s agency in experience and so forth occurs through the grace of His own essential power (*svarūpa-śakti*).

And the Śruti says: "Where everything has become the Self alone for him, by what and whom should he see? (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.4.14). This indicates that without His own essential power (*svarūpa-śakti*), there is no capacity for the perception of Him, as supported by such scriptural passages as: "He is obtained by whomsoever He chooses" (Kaṭha Upaniṣad 1.2.23).
Therefore, when Māyā is withdrawn, those who possess the relationship with the power of the essential nature (svarūpa-śakti) attain the destruction of saṃsāra;
however, for those in whose view there is no experience of bliss in liberation, there is no fulfillment of the purpose of man (pumarthatā).
It is accomplished;
for even if an object exists, it is useless in the absence of its manifestation,
nor is there happiness [without it].
The wish "may I exist" belongs to no one;

rather, [the wish is] simply "I experience happiness. Consequently, since there is an absence of activity [based on that wish], even the impulsion toward the means for achieving such a human goal (puruṣārtha) in the scripture is entirely futile.
In that view, since it is impossible for that which consists solely of the nature of bliss to have a connection with ignorance or suffering,
the human goal (puruṣārtha) consisting of their cessation is not tenable;
yet such a status as a human goal is indeed well-known [in other systems].

In the words of Śrī Nārada addressed to Prācīnabarhiṣ: "The destruction of suffering, the attainment of happiness, and that which is most beneficial—that is not sought here. Therefore, experience certainly exists.
And so says the Śruti:
"For having obtained the essence (rasa), he indeed becomes blissful," and so on, as in "delighting in the Self, sporting with the Self" [Chāndogya Upaniṣad 7.25.2].
As it is stated in the Viṣṇudharma:
"Just as when a leather bag is burst, the air within is no longer distinct from the external air,
so too the self, when its bonds of merit and demerit are exhausted, is not separate from Brahman."
Thereafter, one attains an eternal, stainless, and unique delight, which is the perfection of all auspiciousness and all happiness.
For the Self, whose nature is Brahman, O King of kings, that [bliss] indeed always remains unobscured even at the time of emergence from meditation.
Just as the stainlessness of a mirror shines forth due to the absence of impurities,
so too does that bliss of the self shine forth when that which is to be abandoned has been consumed by the fire of knowledge.
Just as qualities such as awakening and the rest become manifest through the destruction of qualities to be abandoned, yet are not newly produced— for they are indeed eternal attributes of the Self.
O Lord of Men, knowledge, dispassion, sovereignty, and virtue—
these four are eternally present in the Self which has become Brahman.
"This non-duality has been declared; this very [truth] has been taught to you:

'This is Viṣṇu, this is Brahman, and likewise this is the supreme reality. In this context, the analogy of the wind is given precisely because of the relationship of part and whole between the individual soul (jīva) and Brahman. Even though it is a part, [the soul is not different from the whole].
Its being external, however, is to be understood from other sources. Therefore, when there is the experience of the Lord's own nature as distinct [from the self],
the Māyā of the Lord— having obtained an opening through that ancient aversion— [obstructs] that experience.
Because the possibility of dissolution and so forth exists, there is a cessation [of the breaths] through some means by way of that favoring [the self],
according to such scriptural passages as, "The knower of the bliss of Brahman" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.4.1).
Therefore, the vital breaths do not depart from him.

In the passage, "They depart from here; they are merged right here; being Brahman, one goes to Brahman" (BAU 4.4.6), it is also clearly stated that the state of being Brahman is one thing, while the merging into Brahman is another. Brahman—
Because that dissolution is mentioned immediately after existence,
and because Brahman is designated as the object of the verbal root *api* (to dissolve).
And thus, in the phrase "being Brahman itself," the designation of non-difference is made through the attainment of equality with that and identity with that.
Likewise, [it is said]: "He who knows Brahman becomes Brahman itself" (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 3.2.8).
This too should be explained here;
in some places it is expressed in the same way even by the word "oneness.
Regarding this, that similarity is as stated:
"In the Śruti, such as *nirañjanaṃ parama-sāmyam upaiti* (Mundaka Upanishad 3.2.3), it is said: 'Having taken refuge in this knowledge, they have attained my own nature. (Page 8)
Thus it is said in the Gītā Upaniṣad;
and both points have been stated quite clearly:
"As pure water poured into pure water becomes exactly like that."

"Thus, O Gautama, the self of the sage who knows becomes [one with Brahman]. In that very context, by the word "thus" (eva), it is indicated that it does not become that [Brahman] itself, nor is it perceived as something separate due to a lack of similarity to it. And in the Skanda Purāṇa:
Just as water poured into water becomes indeed mixed,
that very thing remains as it is from which cognition proceeds.

"In this very way, although the individual soul (jīva) has attained identity with the Supreme Self (paramātman), it does not become that [Self], because of its specific attributes such as independence [and so forth].
This is the explanation of the reflection and its prototype, beginning with the sūtra: "And [the reflection is like] the cloud," and so on. (Vs. 3.2.19) etc.
In both cases, it is applied only in a secondary sense;

for this very reason, even in the passage, "This serene being, having arisen from this body and having reached the highest light, appears in its own true form" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.12.3), it is likewise so.
In the same way, the distinction is established;

even in the *Śrī Viṣṇu Purāṇa*, in passages such as "when ignorance, which generates the distinctions, has perished" (*ViP* 6.7.84), it is shown that after the destruction of the distinctions of gods and so forth, there remains the identity of Brahman and the self.
It has already been explained that no one will bring about a non-existent division, but rather they will bring about one that is indeed existent;
this is precisely what is accepted by the authors of the *Ṭīkā*s following the attainment of Brahman by the venerable cowherds (*śrī-gopāḥ*).
Or rather, there is even the vision of Vaikuṇṭha.
Therefore, it has been correctly explained by the passage beginning with "If he has ceased...
(BhP 1.3.34). Thus, the attainment of Brahman has been explained.
In that regard, in the *Śrī Viṣṇu Purāṇa*, within the determination of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-nirṇaya*), there is the speech of Jaḍa-bharata addressed to Rahūgaṇa; therein,
it is determined that the experience of absolute Brahman alone is the ultimate truth.

The non-ultimate nature of the *apūrva* resulting from sacrifices and the like has been stated by the four [authorities]. "In your view, the sacrificial act accomplished through the *Ṛg*, *Yajur*, and *Sāma* Vedas is considered the ultimate reality; even regarding that, listen as I speak."
Whatever effect is produced from clay as its material cause,
O King, that [effect] arises as being made of clay, because it follows the nature of its cause.
In this way, whatever action is accomplished by means of perishable substances such as fuel-sticks, clarified butter, and kuśa grass,
that action itself must be perishable.
"The wise accept that the ultimate reality (paramārtha) is imperishable;
however, that which is produced by perishable substances is perishable, without a doubt.
By this analogy, it should not be inferred that devotion consisting of worship and the like is also of such a nature.
Because devotion that is unprecedented cannot be produced;
for that which is produced must consist of qualities, not that which is devoid of qualities.
Beginning with the statement, "Kaivalya is sattvic knowledge" (BhP 11.25.24),
the Blessed Lord Himself has affirmed in the Eleventh Canto that it is devoid of the material modes (*aguṇamaya*).
Therefore, regarding the power of His own essential nature (*svarūpa-śakti*)—
Because it is a specific mode of manifestation (*vṛtti-viśeṣa*), when there is the grace of the Blessed One, its appearance is simply a self-manifestation and not a birth.
Furthermore, that manifestation is indeed infinite, because its fruits are heard to be infinite. Therefore:

In that case, "not having the Supreme Lord as its refuge" will serve as the limiting condition (upādhi) for the inference that sin arises from violence, just as "not being prescribed by scripture" is a condition for [the inference regarding] killing.
And since devotion is not the subject introduced in this section on knowledge (*jñāna*),
this engagement proceeds by taking recourse to common sacrifices and the like;
thus, [the path] beginning with sacrifice—

Having stated that ritual action (*karman*) is not ultimately real because its unseen potency (*apūrva*) is perishable, one [verse] has further stated that even desireless action is likewise [not ultimately real], since it is merely a means for achieving another end: "That very action which yields no fruit is, in Your view, considered the ultimate reality."
"Because it is the means for achieving liberation, the ultimate reality is not itself a means.
(ViP 2.14.25) In this regard, one should not consider devotion to be such [an ultimate reality] in its capacity as a means; rather, it is love for the Blessed Lord.
Since it is heard that even for the Siddhas, who have attained perfection, there is no abandonment of that [body] because it is of the nature of their graceful play (vilāsa),
this too should be understood as being like the previous case.

Now, one might object that meditation on the pure individual soul (jīvātman) must be the ultimate reality, because its nature is imperishable, as it is admitted to manifest even in the state of liberation.
And because it is now called "saṃsāra" due to being covered by that [ignorance], and because that very [ignorance] is what is to be accomplished [overcome],
it has been stated therein by one [author]:

"O King, if meditation (dhyāna) is what is designated by the term 'the ultimate reality' (paramārtha) for the self, then that ultimate reality is not characterized by difference from others who cause division. Thus,
that very Brahman through the knowledge of which the knowledge of all things arises is the ultimate reality (paramārtha) according to the Śruti.
It has been asserted that he consists of all consciousness because he is the self of all; for fire-consciousness is indeed...
It serves as a communicator even for things such as flames and sparks;

however, since a single individual soul possesses the state of being an atom characterized by a portion of its own vital power (*jīva-śakti*), there exists a distinction between that [atom] and its manifestation.
The meaning is that this is not the ultimate reality (*paramārthatva*).

Now, one might object: when an absolute union is manifested through the contemplation of the coexistence of the individual self (*jīvātman*) and the supreme self (*paramātman*) in a single locus, would that [union] not also exist in its entirety?
Otherwise, the consequence would be their non-difference;
and that conjunction is not perishable.
Because it is established immediately after [the attainment of] knowledge;
therefore, let the union of those two alone be the ultimate reality. Regarding this, it was said by one [author]:

"The union of the supreme self and the individual self is held to be the ultimate reality; this is false, for one substance does not become the substance of another. (ViP 2.14.27) The meaning is that this status of being the ultimate reality is itself considered false.
Indeed, it is certain;

because [it is so], that other substance characterized as the individual soul (*jīva*) does not possess the nature of that substance— the nature of the substance characterized as the Supreme Self (*paramātman*).

It departs. Therefore, just as a small light enters into a great light, because there is no possibility of non-difference even through absolute conjunction (*atyanta-saṃyoga*), the sense is that their conjunction (*yoga*) is not ultimately real (*paramārtha*).
Alternatively, here [the term] *yoga*—
By the word "one," unity itself is expressed;
therefore, this should be explained as "this unity. The remainder is as before.
Thus, having refuted the prima facie arguments, one person has begun to establish the final position:
"Therefore, O King, all these [virtues] are superior, without a doubt."
"But as for the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), O King, hear it from me in brief. (ViP 2.14.28).
"Welfares" (*śreyāṃsi*) are the means for achieving the ultimate truth;
the exposition of the ultimate truth has been stated by way of a triad.
The Self is one, all-pervading, equal, pure, devoid of qualities, beyond primordial nature (prakṛti),
free from birth, growth, and so forth, omnipresent, and immutable.

O King, that all-pervading Lord was never ununited with supreme knowledge, nor was he ever unjoined with it through the unreal designations of names, classes, and so forth; indeed, he has never been otherwise, nor will he ever be.

"That which is indeed of a single nature, existing within his own body and the bodies of others—that consciousness is the ultimate reality (paramārtha); it is not for one who perceives duality, which is unreal. Thus, he is "one" (eka), and not many like individual souls (jīvas).
It is "all-pervading" (*vyāpin*) because it pervades all its own powers and all its own effects, just as fire pervades its flames and sparks.
By the term "all-reaching" (*sarva-gata*), it is indicated that [the Lord] is not non-dual like the individual soul (*jīva*).
It has been made known that [the Self] is all-pervasive by its very power within the body;
moreover, it consists of that knowledge which is superior even to the knowledge of the individual soul (jīva),
and is primarily characterized by its manifestation.

By the qualification "by the non-existent," it is made known that even when the form of the Blessed Lord is the object to be manifested, one becomes possessed of yoga through names and so forth that are "existent" (sat), meaning they are established in their own essential nature.

Of that very Self, characterized in this way, which exists as the nature of the Supreme Self within one's own body and the bodies of others— though appearing as if separate due to the distinctions of their respective limiting adjuncts (upādhis)— that knowledge which realizes its single, own essential nature (*svarūpa*) as being composed of that and having that as its essence; that [knowledge].
This very experience is the ultimate reality,
because it is indestructible and because it is that which is to be realized by all.
The intention is that it is because [the self] is included within consciousness;
however, those who maintain dualism consider even that [consciousness] to be divided according to their perception of various respective limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*).
Furthermore, they do not maintain that all other cognitions are included within that [single] cognition;
rather, they are simply those who perceive what is unreal.
In this regard, although there is a distinction of parts due to the distinctions of limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), non-distinction is established by means of two examples:
Just as the distinction known by the names of *ṣaḍja* and so forth arises from the differentiation of the holes in a flute,
so too does that same distinction apply to the air of that Great Self, though it pervades all without division.
"Unity and the differentiation of forms arise from the engagement in external karma;
those differences such as 'god' and so forth are superimpositions, for that [Brahman] is indeed devoid of activity.
Thus, the syntactical connection is "its unity is likewise."
The differentiation of form into its various shapes, however,

arises from the activity of karma belonging to the individual soul (jīva), which is the external aspect of that [consciousness]. That Supreme Self, presiding over the distinctions such as gods and others solely through its role as the inner ruler (antaryāmī), [remains] within those respective limiting adjuncts (upādhi).
And because there is no connection [between the self and the body], there is simply no obscuration such that one could be "of such a nature";
therefore, the meaning is that his form as a god and so forth consists solely of his own divine play (*sva-līlā*).
Now, he states that the direct perception of the Blessed Lord is liberation:
Then, having avoided from afar the company of Daityas who are devoted to sense-objects,
approach Nārāyaṇa, the primordial God.

"He is the liberation desired by those freed from attachment" (BhP 7.6.18). And the commentary states: "Because he alone is the desired liberation"—in this regard, Nārāyaṇa's nature as liberation [is established].
It culminates precisely in its own direct realization;
for that [realization] alone consists in the attainment of supreme bliss preceded by the destruction of saṃsāra, whereas in its mere existence, such a state is absent.
// 7.6 // Śrī Prahlāda // 5 // [6] Likewise:
O Blessed One, those whose blessings are true indeed [worship] Your lotus feet.

O noble one, may the Blessed Lord, who is the embodiment of the goals of human life and who bestows blessings upon those who worship Him, likewise protect us— the wretched— just as a cow protects her calf, being ever-anxious to show His grace.
And the commentary says: "O Blessed One!
[I bow] to the lotus-foot of Him whose very form is that human goal which is supreme bliss."
Compared to blessings such as sovereignty and the like, the true blessing is the fruit of the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*).
Indeed (*hi*), this is certain. For whom? For you alone, in that manner—that is, in the way that you yourself are the human goal (*puruṣārtha*). Thus [it is said].
For one who worships with desirelessness,
although it is thus, nevertheless [the prayer begins]: "O Noble One, O Lord, even us who are wretched and full of desire," and so forth.
// 4.9 // Dhruva is dear to Śrī-Dhruva.
// 6 // [7] And that direct realization of the Self is twofold: characterized by internal manifestation and external manifestation.
And as for the definition:
"As the Lord of the Tīrthas, whose fame is dear, sang of his own heroic deeds, he quickly entered my heart and appeared there as if summoned" (BhP 1.6.34), and so forth.
They described their own fortune of meditative absorption, which was beyond the range of the eyes.
And so on, as in [BhP 3.15.38].
Regarding that, the fitness for internal direct realization is stated in the *Śrī-rudra-gīta*:
"He whose mind does not experience the delusion of external objects..."
And he entered the pure cave within the darkness; indeed,
O Sage, you perceive the destination there, which is easily reached by those favored by the yoga of devotion.

In this regard, that sage whose previously mentioned mind has been purified by being favored by the yoga of devotion (*bhakti-yoga*), and which neither wanders among external objects nor enters the cave consisting of darkness— that sage, and so forth, is to be explained.
Even regarding external perception, it was stated by the Blessed Lord to Nārada in the same manner through a negative illustration:
"Alas! In this birth, you ought not to see me here;
I am difficult to perceive for those of imperfect spiritual discipline and for those who practice flawed yoga. (BhP 1.6.22)
The capacity [for realization] consists not merely in the purity of mind alone;
what then? It is the manifestation of the power of His own self-luminosity, which consists of the desire for Him manifested through a particular devotion to Him—this indeed is the root.
That is *rūpa*, by whose manifestation even that [unmanifested state] is established in its entirety.

As it is said: "In the internal realization, the knot of the heart is severed" (BhP 1.2.21), and so forth; likewise, in the external realization as well, in the words of Citraketu addressed to Śrī Saṅkarṣaṇa:
"O Blessed One,
it is not the case that for men there is no destruction of all sins through the sight of You," as stated by Śrī Nṛsiṃha to Prahlāda in His own words.
"Therefore, instruct us, your own servants; O Lord, what shall we do?
This is the end of the afflictions of men: that you have come within the range of their vision.
Thus, when the state of the mind being completely purified through His manifestation is established, the instruments of human effort [are employed].
They would possess the conceit of being manifest only by virtue of having attained identity with His power of self-luminosity;
in that regard, it has been stated that there is a dependence upon a particular degree of devotion.
In passages such as "The sages who have faith...
(BhP 1.2.12), and in the illustrative example beginning with "consisting of His will," Brahman and the Blessed Lord are seen to be without any distinction whatsoever.
As stated in the words of the venerable Matsya-deva to Satyavrata:
"And my own majesty is designated by the term 'the Supreme Brahman'."
"You shall know that which has been favored by Me, revealed within Your heart through Your inquiries. (BhP 8.24.38).
Likewise, in the words of the Blessed Lord addressed to Brahmā: "This is the power of one's own contemplation..."
Regarding the statement, "My survey of the worlds" (BhP 2.9.21),
the *Śrī-Nārāyaṇādhyātma* states:
"Although the Lord is eternally unmanifest, He is perceived through His own power."
"Who else but the lotus-eyed one could behold that immeasurable Lord?
And in the Śruti: "He whom this [Self] chooses, by him is He attained; to him this Self reveals His own form. (Kaṭha Upaniṣad 1.2.23)
Therefore, even the requirement for the purification of the instruments [of action] should be understood as being solely for the purpose of reflecting that [divine] power.
Nevertheless, it was proclaimed by the Blessed Lord that even in cases such as Mucukunda, where one has seen Him with devotion, there may still persist sins such as hunting.

That [vision] was indeed created as a mere intimidation for the purpose of increasing her longing— which arose from the sudden fear of not attaining the Lord— by means of *prema-vardhinī*. As for the vision of hell shown to his affectionate ones, such as Śrī Yudhiṣṭhira and others, that was certainly [the work of] Indra.
That it is indeed composed of illusion (māyā-maya) is clearly evident in the Svargārohaṇa-parvan itself;
for even in the case of a Brahmin who has given sesame seeds and cows during his third birth according to the Viṣṇudharma, [he falls] into hells by mere association.
Furthermore, although the attainment of a form equal to that of heaven is described [in other texts],
even that is not accepted by the Śrīmad Bhāgavata.
Because that [state] cannot be described, and because, on the contrary, there is a description of the immediate attainment of the Blessed One;
furthermore, as for the fact that even those with impure minds are heard to have direct realization upon the descent [of the Lord] and so forth, that indeed—
That alone is to be known as its appearance,
according to the Śrī Gītā Upaniṣads: "I am not manifest to everyone, being veiled by my own yoga-māyā" (Gītā 7.25).
He is seen by yogis through devotion;
he is never seen without devotion.
He cannot be seen through anger.
Or from envy, O Janārdana.
And from the *Padmottara-khaṇḍa* [of the *Padmapurāṇa*], 6.238.83:
"Non-perception" means the absence of perception even of the all-pervading one at a time when there is no incarnation (*avatāra*), whereas at the time of an incarnation...
Furthermore, even in supreme bliss there is the giving of suffering; even in what is delightful there is terror; [and] toward every friend...
Even such misconceptions as "He is ill-behaved" and so forth are merely perverted views;
and the root cause for the non-manifestation of Him and the manifestation of *yoga-māyā* is the person consisting of offenses against His devotees and the like.
The transparency of the mind;
indeed, that which at that time remains as if indelibly fixed, even amidst its universal manifestation.

Therefore, because the definition [of liberation] beginning with "liberation is [attained] by abandoning" (BhP 2.10.6) suffers from the fault of being under-extensive (*avyāpti*), that semblance of direct realization cannot even be designated as "liberation.
For this very reason, in the *Śrī Viṣṇu Purāṇa*, that...

Although the vision of Śiśupāla regarding Him was described by the prose passage beginning with "And he saw His form" (ViP 4.15.8), nevertheless, that vision as being free from defects is said to occur only at the time of death,
for the purpose of his own destruction.

This is indicated by the passage: "He beheld the Blessed One, who had become Brahman, whose nature is imperishable splendor, radiant with the garland of rays from the discus in the Lord's hand, and free from defects such as hatred" (ViP 4.15.9);
and also by the verse beginning: "The affliction of men ends when you come within the range of their vision" (BhP 10.83.43).
Among men, for those whose minds are pure and for those whose minds are stained by faults other than offenses against His devotees,
there is the destruction of their afflictions with regard to the immediate present; however, for those who are otherwise, [there is the destruction of their afflictions] through that—

This is precisely because of the expectation of their imminent destruction, as heard in the scripture: "To them, whose eyes had their darkness destroyed by the sight of Him, the Teacher of the three worlds granted security and the vision of the ultimate goal" (BhP 10.83.81), and in accordance with the *Śrī Viṣṇu Purāṇa* and other texts.
And those with impure minds are of two kinds: those who turn away from the Blessed One and those who hate the Blessed One.
Those who turn away from Him are also of two kinds: those who, even though they have obtained the sight of Him, remain attached to sense objects and the like, and those who treat Him with contempt.
Just as at the time of His descent, common gods, humans, and others [were present],
and as it is said: "Having taken recourse to Kṛṣṇa, who is mortal," and so forth.
Mahendra and the others are difficult to address [with such words],
since it has been said by the Vedas:
"Those who fix their minds even once upon You, the Self who is eternal bliss..."
"But they do not again resort to dwellings that carry away the essence of man.
Thus [it was said]. And regarding Mahendra, the Blessed Lord said:
"Blinded by the intoxication of power and prosperity, he does not see me, the wielder of the staff."
"I deprive him of his prosperity whom I wish to favor.
In the case of the illustrious cowherds, however, their connection with sense objects was not for their own sake,
but rather for the purpose of facilitating their service to Him.
Thus, as it is said:
"Abode, wealth, friends, beloved, self, son, life, and hope—for Your sake" (BhP 10.14.35); and "Those who have dedicated their self, friends, wealth, wife, and desires to Kṛṣṇa" (BhP).

Thus it is said: "Kṛṣṇa, whose eyes are like lotus petals, whose hearing and chanting are meritorious" (BhP 10.15.42). Furthermore, even the relationship between Śrī Kṛṣṇa and the Yādavas and Pāṇḍavas appears as if it were for His own sake.
As it has been said:
"In sleeping, sitting, walking, conversing, playing, bathing, eating, and so forth, the Vṛṣṇis—whose minds are fixed on Kṛṣṇa—do not perceive their own selves, though they exist. [BhP 10.90.46]
"O twice-born ones, did those desires so coveted by the gods bring any joy to King Mukundadeva’s mind, as other things might bring joy to a hungry man? (BhP 1.12.6).
Therefore, [the Lord spoke] such words as: "For those thus attached to their homes and intoxicated by the pursuit of them... (BhP 1.13.17), and so forth.
This was said with reference to Dhṛtarāṣṭra and the others who were characterized by that [name], through the figure of indication (jahad-lakṣaṇā).
For this very reason, immediately thereafter, Vidura, intending that same point, spoke in [BhP 1.13.18] and so forth.
Thus, the instruction is intended for Dhṛtarāṣṭra alone.
But it does not belong to them either; and in some cases,

the power of divine play (līlā-śakti) itself, for the sake of nourishing the sweetness of that play, deposits such power within those who are unfavorable as well as favorable to themselves— among those very persons dear to Him— acting as His own instruments.
It even produces the appearance of being possessed by sense objects,
as in the description of Pūtanā: "She who captivated the minds of the inhabitants of Vraja with her charming smiles, side-long glances, and looks" (BhP).

Thus [it is said]. And with the intention of expressing that she is a mere semblance of her, it was stated by the learned author as "captivating the mind, acting as if she were the Mind-Captivator herself" (*mano-harā ivācarantīm*). Furthermore, the fact that her power is granted by him is indicated in that very same place:—
For it is said: "Indeed, there the female demons do not perform the demon-slaying rites of hearing and so forth for their own purposes in the presence of the Lord of the Sātvatas" (BhP 10.6.3).
It is in this very way that this [situation] is consistent.

"The gopīs thought of Him, who was like the goddess Śrī in embodied form, as if He were their husband come to see them with His lotus-hand—Śrī being the presiding deity over material opulence, and He being her husband according to some previous [karmic connection].
[BhP 10.6.6] Thus [it is said]. Śrī is the presiding deity of material prosperity (prākṛta-sampat). Her husband is anyone suitable for her based on former [deeds].
The meaning is "one who partakes of merit.

Just as before, in the passage beginning with "that sharp-minded one" (BhP 10.6.9), while he was being gazed upon after she had been overwhelmed by her radiance, his two mothers indeed stood still. (BhP)
Thus it has been said.
In exactly the same way, one should understand that in certain instances there is even the appearance of the subjugation of such [beings] by *māyā*, as in passages such as:
"Generally, the *māyā* of my Lord does not delude even me" (BhP 10.13.37), and so forth.
[This refers to] those such as Śrī Baladeva and others;
for example, [it was so] with Jaya and Vijaya at their birth as Daityas.
In this case, the reflection of the former [state] is only slight.
However, the distinction between those two lies in the term "correctly":
it is due to the absence of obscuration and the presence of obscuration regarding love and the other [virtues].
In that regard, when those two have reached a state of enmity—
Indeed, there would not be the state of being composed by a sage;
for in the verse "But this is my opinion" (BhP 3.16.29), the Lord's will is established as the cause thereof.
Nor does that [pleasure] lead to enmity toward Him, because He is composed of His own will; and because of such statements as,

"O Śakra, our Lord ordains for a person the destruction of the exertions pertaining to the three aims of life" (BhP 10.14.2), there arises the implication by way of *kaimutya* (the principle of "how much more so").

And as it has been said: "O Mādhava, those who have bound their friendship to You never fall from the path anywhere" (BhP 10.2.33). Nor should it be argued that even for the sake of quickly delivering those two from the experience of their own offense, such a desire arose in Him.
For such supreme devotees, indeed, without devotion they do not accept even *sālokya* and other forms of liberation;
yet, when that [devotion] exists, they accept even hell— thus they do not consider [liberation] as ultimate.
This is based on such passages as [BhP 3.15.48], and also from [BhP 3.15.49]: "Let there be for us, by our own sins, birth in the hells at will," and so forth.
For this very reason, they both likewise prayed in that same manner.

By the verse, "May there not arise in you a trace of remorse that destroys the remembrance of the Blessed One, while we two go further and further down," it is shown that if a state of actual enmity existed between those two, happiness would not accrue even to other devotees.
This must be stated: it is precisely because of the contradiction between the nature of devotion and the affection of a devotee that there arises the manifestation of a state of enmity between them.
Therefore, it is only through this semblance of hostility between the two that the arising of rasa occurs for the Śrī Bhagavān, as well as for His other devotees.
Thus it is established.

Therefore, for this very reason, [the Lord acts] by means of what is obtained through presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) in order to accomplish the delight of battle and other such things desired by the Blessed One, which grant happiness to all who partake [of His grace].

Having entered the illusory adjunct consisting of the nature of enmity by means of their own pure-sattva bodies endowed with powers such as *aṇimā*, and having made it their own through their presence and having dissolved [the adjunct] while remaining there,
they remain even while that latent impression of devotion (*bhakti-vāsanā*) persists, yet they do not become possessed by it. Therefore—

By the recollection of that which arises from a state of enmity, the state of enmity departs; thus both are external. With this very intention, even the venerable Lord Vaikuṇṭha said: "Go, do not fear; let there be peace" (BhP 3.16.29).

For instance, in the battle with Hiraṇyākṣa, regarding the verse beginning with *parānuṣaktam* (BhP 3.18.9), the commentary states: "The state of fierce anger and the insults and so forth are merely a simulation, intended to dispel the fear of the gods who were terrified by the words of the Daityas."
In reality, because he did not speak in that manner, there was no cause for anger or the like;
this is the sense in the verse beginning with "karālā" (BhP 3.19.8), where the word "iva" (as if) is used in its actual sense.
The absence of anger is this [state].
Thus, even in the Syamantaka episode, the Mahākālapura episode,
the Mausala episode, and others, there was an onset of anger and so forth on the part of Śrī Baladeva, Arjuna, Nārada, and the rest.
He should be reconciled with them by means of even a mere trace of that semblance.

In this regard, the distinction is as follows: Śrī Baladeva, Arjuna, and others [were reconciled] through their knowledge of the Blessed Lord’s intention, whereas Śrī Nārada and others were reconciled through their direct knowledge of it—thus was he provoked to anger.
"The sages, experts in the doctrines of the Blessed One, spoke thus"— this is from the words of Śrī Uddhava in the Third Canto [of the Bhāgavata Purāṇa].
Therefore, for those whose direct realization is indeed perfected through another sign (liṅga),...
In those cases where it is understood that their internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) is not pure, even though this is being perceived, it is merely a semblance (*ābhāsa*) of that [knowledge].
However, for those in whom it is not understood [to be impure] and who are seen to be possessed by objects and so forth, there is a semblance of direct realization (*sākṣātkārābhāsa*).
Thus it has been determined. Therefore, it has been stated that those with turbid minds do not see, even though they look outward.
And those who hate Him are of two kinds:

some perceive His beauty and so forth, yet because they do not perceive His sweetness, they hate Him due to a lack of relish for that very same [beauty], just as Kālayavana and others did; while others, however—
They perceive it as a mere transformation and consequently feel aversion toward it, just as wrestlers and others do.
Thus, in all four of these preceding and subsequent cases, those with tongues afflicted by defects serve as examples of partial eaters.
For some, being possessed of defects born of bile and wind, do not grasp its true flavor; however—
Having applied all their respect, they do not despise it;
yet others, being conceited, even despise it.
Furthermore, others accept this [work] as having a sweet flavor, but those who prefer bitter, sour, and other such tastes reject it.
In this way, some people detest the taste;
others, moreover, perceive it precisely as bitter and likewise detest it. This applies to all [of them].
For them, these [perceptions] possess the nature of being mere semblances (*tad-ābhāsatva*), like the fragmented apprehension of an object obstructed by one's own defects.

Furthermore, their experience of the Lord’s essential nature is indeed logical, given the absence of knowledge, devotion, pure love, and the characteristics of His absolute sovereignty and supreme sweetness— namely, His being *sat*, *cit*, and *ānanda*.
Because it is impossible to grasp intrinsic natures,
even if they are not grasped, liberation at a later time should be understood as being like the consumption of a medicinal powder.

nevertheless, that [state] characterized by manifest appearance is distinct from the Brahman characterized by non-manifest appearance, which is like deep sleep (*suṣupti*).
It differs from *sāyujya* (union).
