Attachment (*rāga*) is affection itself, characterized by an excess of longing.
Upon his birth,
even a momentary separation became utterly unbearable;
yet, in union with him, even supreme suffering was endured.
It appears as pleasure;
in its absence, it is the opposite.
That very passion, at every moment, [perceives] its own object...
Anurāga is that which, experiencing itself as ever-new and becoming ever-fresh,
results upon its arising in an excellence of mutual subordination;
it is a state of affectionate transformation directed toward a non-living object related to that [living being].
Even a longing for rebirth arises,
as does an outburst during separation;
indeed, passion itself is unsurpassed.
The great state (*mahābhāva*) is intoxicating through its wonder;
when that yoga arises,
there occurs such things as the inability to endure even a blink of an eye, the perception of an eon as a single moment, and so forth.
In separation, a single moment becomes like an eon, and so forth;
in both cases, all the highly inflamed transformations of the *sattva* quality and the rest arise. Thus, the qualities that serve as the causes for latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) have been shown.

Now, the qualities that serve as specific causes for the pride of being a devotee, and the resulting distinctions and gradations among devotees in their love, are as follows: indeed, that very same love, upon attaining a connection with the manifestation of a particular nature of the Blessed One, regards someone as an object of grace and [regards] another... [as such].
Out of compassion for some, out of friendship for others, and out of affection for yet others,
[he manifests] the nature of the Blessed One.

Furthermore, the cause for the manifestation of excellence in that particular beloved of the Blessed One— namely, the joy obtained through association and so forth— is to be understood as a specific quality of that very joy;
this is eternally so for those who are eternal attendants.

That is twofold. Among these, the joy consisting of the conceit of being one who is favored is well known by the term *bhakti*. For it is consistent with that [definition] that "knowledge of [the Lord] as the object of worship is *bhakti*. As it has been said:
"In the manifestation of Māyā, that attachment which is preceded by great esteem is called devotion; that alone is the cause for [attaining] the Supreme Lord. Thus [it is said].
In this context, "affection" (sneha) means mere love. Thus, it is said in the Padma Purāṇa: "Devotion is defined as the cognition of greatness preceded by affection."
Nevertheless, it was stated previously that because devotion toward the Blessed One is a synonym for "affection" (*prīti*) in general, the sages employ the word "devotion" (*bhakti*) [in that sense].
In some cases, even words denoting a specific quality are used in a general sense.
They are applied to the generality of a living being, like the words "king" or "servant";
in some cases, due to an excess of figurative application (bhakti).

The application of the word "bhakti" even to that which possesses the [mere] characteristics [of devotion] is like calling someone a "Brāhmaṇa" in Brāhmaṇa assemblies when he merely possesses an excellence of Brāhmaṇahood;
as it has been said in the Pāñcarātra:

"But that affection which is preceded by knowledge of [His] greatness, which is very firm and superior in every respect, is called *bhakti*; through it, [one attains] equality with Him (*sārṣṭya*) and so forth, and not otherwise.
However, in some instances, the word *bhakti* is used for the movement of the mind and similar functions solely because of their connection with that [affection].
The state of being expressible has been stated.
Affection consisting of the conceit of being favored by that [Lord] is indeed the primary meaning of the word "bhakti."
And those who possess the conceit of being benefactors are of two kinds,
because there are two types of assistance: nourishing and compassion.
In this context, "nourishing" (poṣaṇa) refers to the Blessed One’s act of gladdening [the devotee] by means of His own form and His own qualities;
and "compassion" (anukampā) refers to [His action] even though He is already complete in Himself, on account of His own service and so forth.

It is the Lord’s desire to benefit those two types of persons— consisting of a moistening of His heart— which, by fulfilling their aspirations, brings about for them, among their servants and others, the good fortune of service and so forth;
[this desire] resides in the Lord toward some among those two kinds of persons.
They are free from possessiveness and equal toward all.

Among them, those who take pride in being delighted by the Blessed One through the realization that He is the Supreme Self and the Supreme Brahman are the jñānī-bhaktas, such as the venerable Sanaka and others, who are free from possessiveness.

Even though they possess that conceit, there is an absence of the sense of "mine" regarding it—just as in the verse: "O Lord, even though the distinction has vanished, I am not yours, nor are you mine; for a wave belongs to the ocean, yet the ocean is not the wave."
Just as for you there is the sight of the moon, their vision of the Blessed One would be a source of joy even without personal attachment (*mamatā*).
Furthermore, "conformity" (*ānukūlya*) here is to be understood through such acts as being inclined toward Him, praising Him, and so forth.
And their joy—
It is called knowledge-devotion (*jñāna-bhakti*); its nature as knowledge arises from experiencing it as the very density of Brahman. This same state is also designated by the name "peace" (*śānti*).
Because tranquility (*śama*) is predominant; for there is a statement by the Blessed One: "Tranquility is the mind's abiding in the *Man*. [BhP 11.19.36]
Furthermore, those who are worthy of compassion are impartial devotees;
for in them, a sense of possessiveness has arisen through the thought, "This one is our master."

With this very intention, the quality of speaking such words as "having no sense of 'mine' for anything else" and so forth was declared only of the exclusive devotees— namely Śrī Bhīṣma, Uddhava, Prahlāda, Nārada, and others— and not even of Sanaka and the rest.
Therefore, precisely because they arise from the sense of "mine," those who possess that conceit are objects of compassion.
This state of being worthy of compassion is threefold:
the state of being one to be protected, the state of being a servant, and the state of being one to be cherished.

Among them, according to their threefold nature in sequence, those such as the citizens of Dvārakā possess the sentiment (*bhāva*) toward the Blessed Lord as "Protector" (*pālaka*); those such as the servants headed by Śrī Dāruka possess the sentiment as "One to be served" (*sevya*); and those such as Śrī Pradyumna and Gada possess the sentiment as "Teacher" (*guru*).
Starting with the sons, such as Nṛja and the others—
among these three types as well, love is indeed devotion;
and compared to the former, because their love possesses a greater degree of conformity to [the object], it is superior.
Because it is a portion of the knowledge of Truth (*ṛta*), this very [state] has been given the name "affection" (*prīti*) in this very *Śrī-Rasāmṛta-Sindhu* (page 47).
And that devotion (*bhakti*) is, in due order, of the nature of a refuge for those to be protected and of service for those who are servants.
That which consists of the nature of a servant should be known as having the nature of humility toward those who are to be cherished;
whereas that which [arises] from the notion of greatness...
Devotion characterized by mental respect is manifested through acts such as prostration; since that is indeed not [the same as] affection (*prīti*), it is not counted here.
If, however, there were an affection consisting solely of respect, even in the absence of those various states [of devotion], [it would be distinct].
It should be understood as a form of devotion in general.
Furthermore, *vātsalya* is the affection consisting of the conceit of having felt compassion through such thoughts as "this is my son";
for the etymological derivation—that it takes (*lāti*) the child (*vatsam*) to its breast (*vakṣas*)—conveys an immediate understanding of that very state.
But when it refers merely to joy, the application [of the term] is solely by way of indicating that;
and some who know worldly aesthetic flavor (rasa) apply it to this very [joy].
They consider the aesthetic sentiment (rasa) named *vatsala* [the parental affection].
Thus it is illustrated by the venerable Devahūti during her separation from her son: "O child, I am like a cow longing for its calf" (*BhP* 3.33.21).
Therefore, there is the affection (*vātsalya*) of the queens of Śrī-Vraja;

then, by the thought that [the Lord] possesses a sweetness of character and speech equal to one's own, and is the unique refuge of unconditional love, there arises the affection consisting of the conceit of friendship (*mitratva-abhimāna-mayī prītiḥ*), which is called "friendliness" (*maitrī*). Thus, these two types of affection exist toward one another.
That which consists of the delight in providing benefit without any ulterior motive is called *sauhṛda* (friendliness);
and that which consists of affection characterized by dwelling together is called *sakhya* (companionship).
Furthermore, friends are of two kinds:
well-wishers (*suhṛd*) and companions (*sakha*).
Among these, affection (*sauhṛda*) exists in part toward Śrī Yudhiṣṭhira, Bhīṣma, Draupadī, Pādyā, and others.
Friendship is seen toward Śrīmad Arjuna, Śrīdāmā, and others;
whereas the affection arising from the thought "He is my beloved" is the state of being a lover (*kānta-bhāva*).
This very same [affection] is expressed by the term *priyatā* (dearness) in relation to Śrī...
In the *Rasāmṛtasindhu*,
it is defined by worldly connoisseurs as follows: "The state of being dear is *priyatā*."
In this very context, the designation "pleasure" (rati) is accepted;
for this [devotion] is identical to desire, it is also referred to by such terms as "desire" (kāma) with respect to the illustrious gopīs.

But *smara*, known as a specific form of desire (*kāma*), is distinct because of its unique characteristics. For desire in its general sense consists essentially of longing (*spṛhā*), whereas pleasure (*prīti*) is the general sense [of the other].

It is defined as a specific type of cognition consisting of a longing for objects that follow from them, characterized by a nature of conformity to those objects. Therefore, although both [kama and raga] generally consist of activity, the activity of *kāma* (desire) specifically has as its aim one's own personal conformity [to the object].
In that regard, since in some instances the conformity of objects is merely a means to one's own happiness, the word "prīti" (pleasure) is used there only in a secondary sense;
[this applies] only to pure pleasure (*śuddha-prīti*).
Action, however, consists solely in the intent to conform to what is dear;
since one's own happiness follows that very [action], the word "prīti" (pleasure) is used here in its primary sense.

Therefore, just as previously it was shown that although pleasure (*sukha*) and the general state of joy (*prīti-sāmānya*) are similar in their nature as manifestations of exaltation, the general state of joy is distinguished by its aspect of favorability (*ānukūlya*);
so too [is the distinction between] desire (*kāma*) and joy (*prīti*).

Even though the two universals are equal insofar as they consist of specific forms of longing, their distinctiveness is established by that very fact. In this regard, however, [the devotees say]: "O Beloved, we place your well-formed lotus feet upon our breasts slowly, for we are afraid of their hardness" (BhP 10.31.19); thus, even by transgressing [the bounds of propriety], they demonstrate their own favorable disposition.

Since it has been demonstrated that the purport [of the scripture] consists precisely in being favorable toward the Beloved, it follows that [the nature of the goal] is indeed the specific form of pure love (*śuddha-prīti*).

Therefore, its specific nature is established because it consists of a specific kind of longing. Consequently, in this context, since it has Śrī Kṛṣṇa as its object, even if one were not to accept that it is a non-material desire— just like the desire of Kubjā and others directed toward Him— it would follow all the more clearly that it is indeed a material desire.
This is unestablished; and it has been shown thus:
"Whoever, endowed with faith, should hear or describe this playful sport of Viṣṇu performed by the women of Vraja..."
"Having obtained supreme devotion for the Blessed One, the wise man quickly casts off desire, that disease of the heart, in no long time"— by this [verse],
it is shown that even the divine play (vikrīḍita), which reaches others through the gateway of one's own ears despite distance of place and time...
Even for those who are already established [in that state], it swiftly removes whatever desire there may be and extends supreme love;
yet that [state] would not consist of desire,
but rather is a particular form of supreme love.
It is we ourselves; for mud is not washed away by mud,
nor does that which is itself without moisture provide moisture.
Therefore, having described that state as being composed of pure love through direct narration, he further showed that divine grace is the cause of its purity;
the Lord said, "Having seen them..."
Regarding the phrase "gratified by pure devotion" (BhP 10.22.1),
His delight with that jewel among those who find joy in the Self is demonstrated by such passages as "having made Himself so large" (BhP 10.33.19) and others.

And his state of being self-subdued has been demonstrated by himself through such passages as, "I am not able [to restrain myself] from those joined with faultless union" (BhP 10.32.22) and so forth. In that context, the word "niravadya" (faultless) indicates the purity of his love;
this is his own meritorious deed.
It is the state of being supremely excellent and most sublime.
"Na pāraya" means the state of being under one's own mastery.
Therefore, it is pure—
Because his love is supreme among all types of love, even the illustrious Uddhava has said this:
"That which the sages and we ourselves desire out of fear of worldly existence" (BhP 10.47.58).
Therefore, in every respect...
It is established that supreme love (*prīti*) consists of the state of being beloved (*kānta-bhāva*).

Thus, there are five kinds of love according to the distinction between the pride of those states: namely, love as knowledge (*jñāna-bhakti*), devotion (*bhakti*), parental affection (*vātsalya*), friendship (*maitrī*), and the state of being beloved (*kānta-bhāva*).
Furthermore, these qualities such as knowledge and devotion sometimes exist in a mixed state;
among them, in the case of the venerable Bhīṣma and others, there is the basis of both knowledge and devotion.

Devotion to Śrī Yudhiṣṭhira consists of affection and is included within the categories of sheltering devotion (*āśraya-bhakti*) and parental affection (*vātsalya*); friendship toward Śrī Bhīma is also included therein;
and parental affection toward Śrī Kuntī is included within sheltering devotion.
Because of the way [the Lord] manifests His general affection for devotion toward Śrī Vasudeva and Devakī,
as well as in that same manner,
Śrī Uddhava’s friendship— which is included within servitude— is expressed as: "You are My servant, friend, and companion."
Thus it is stated by the Blessed Lord in Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam (11.11.48). Regarding the devotional services of friendship (*sakhya*) and parental affection (*vātsalya*) toward Śrī Baladeva,
therein are friendship and parental affection:
Sometimes, when the Noble One is exhausted from play, she herself rests him by massaging his feet and other such services, while he uses the lap of a cowherd as a pillow.

In passages such as: "While they were dancing, singing, leaping about here and there, and fighting with one another, the two of them, holding hands, laughed and praised the cowherds" (BhP 10.15.14–15), and so forth;
and devotion is evident in their own utterances, such as: "May there be devotion to my Lord, who is Māyā" (BhP 10.13.37), and so forth. In this regard:

And because within the cowherd settlement (vraja), which has become part of His friends, there is the manifestation of pastimes consisting of the revelation of His sovereignty through parental affection and friendship;
therefore, His status as the elder brother in the vraja and the brotherhood of the two sons of Śrī Vasudeva [are established].
Because of his renown, and because he was protected as a son by the illustrious Nanda; as it has been said:
"O brother, is my son with his mother in your Vraja?"
"Thinking of you as my father, I was cherished by both of you. And:
"These boys are indeed your followers; even this one is your elder brother.
Thus, toward the illustrious principal queens, there is the mood of the beloved mixed with servitude (*dāsya*).
Regarding the illustrious queens of Vraja,

it should be understood that their love is mixed with friendship and so forth. Now, however, that affection which exists among the gopīs, characterized by the pride of identifying with those respective emotions, is called "common" (sāmānyā).
It occurs for those who are unfit for such [attainment],
as in the case of the journey to Mithilā—
[passing through] Ānarta, Dhanva, Kuru, Jāṅgala, Kaṅka, Matsya, and so forth.

"O King, the Pāñcālas, Kuntis, Madhus, Kekayas, Kośalas, and others— the men and women among them— drank in with their eyes His lotus-like face, adorned with a noble smile and tender glances. Thus it is said here.
Of some;
and these should be known as being without possessiveness (*nirmama*). Furthermore, regarding those dear to the Blessed One, there is a common tranquility (*sāmānya-śānti*) among them.
These two are called "indifferent" (taṭastha); their affection is also called "indifferent. Among them, there are the protector and the servant.
The two [types of] followers are those whose devotion is known as "respectful affection" (*sambhrama-prīti*).
The dependents (*lālya*) and others, however, are kinsmen; their affection is to be understood as "affection based on kinship" (*bāndhavatā-prīti*).
By these various types of affection,
the different degrees of His own worthiness of worship toward various beloved ones have been described, as in: "To whom I am dear as a self,
a son, a friend, a teacher, a well-wisher, and a chosen deity" (BhP 3.25.38).
The beloved is the lover;
the self is the Supreme Self;
the son consists of sons, brothers, sisters, and so forth, as well as younger siblings; and the friend.
One who plays together with affection is one who takes the form of a teacher, father, or similar figure. Friends are of two kinds.
[These are] relatives and those who act for one's benefit without ulterior motive.
Among these, because the former are included within [the category of] being dear and so forth, the latter are [separately] grasped.
The meaning is that destiny (daiva) is desired, to be resorted to, and to be served;
the sense is that [the hero] is an object of general affection even apart from these [specific] emotional states (bhāvas).
Now, the previously mentioned emotions such as love (rati) and so forth are illustrated.
Regarding that, he speaks of his delight:
"There, day after day, by his grace, I heard the enchanting narrations of Kṛṣṇa as they were being sung."
O dear one, as I listened to those words of Priyaśravas with faith, step by step, a desire arose within me.
O Mahāmati, at that time, my mind became unshakable through its devotion to Priyaśravas,
by which [mind] I perceived this world of existence and non-existence as my own illusion.
"Behold me, the Supreme Brahman, in whom [the world] is imagined.
In me, the pure individual soul (*jīva*), the individual form (*vyaṣṭi-rūpa*) is superimposed; and in the Supreme Brahman, the universal form (*samaṣṭi-rūpa*) is superimposed.
// 1.5 // Śrī Nārada said to Śrī Vyāsa: 84. [85] He spoke of her love:
"O sinless one, you have attained love for your husband and the virtue of a devoted wife."
"Or rather, because my intellect was not drawn away from Me even though it was being agitated by their words.
(BhP 10.60.51) The Blessed Lord spoke with affection to Queen Rukmiṇī: "The Blessed Kṛṣṇa, having been defeated, carried off Śrīdāmā. (BhP 10.18.24)
Thus it is clear.
// 10.18 // Śrī Śuka said: // 86 // [87] He describes her pride: "Frowning with a single knit brow, overwhelmed by the intensity of her love" (BhP 10.32.6). This is clear.
// 10.32 // Śrī Śuka said: // 87 // [88] He speaks of affection:
Even a wise man who has abandoned evil attachments through the company of the virtuous cannot bring himself to give up [affection].
Hearing even once his fame being proclaimed is delightful.
How could the sons of Pṛthā, whose minds were fixed upon him, endure separation from him through seeing, touching, conversing, sharing a bed, a seat, or a meal?
With unblinking eyes and hearts hurried after him,
they all moved here and there, gazing at him, bound by affection.
Restraining their welling tears out of longing for the son of Devakī as he was departing from their home, the women of the kinsmen cried out, "May no ill fortune befall us! [BhP 1.10.11–14] (page 50)
They wandered here and there, moving about for the purpose of bringing offerings and the like;
because an inauspicious omen had occurred at the time of their departure, the women covered [the ground] and blocked the way.
// 1.10 // The Illustrious Sūta said: // 88 // [89] He speaks of passion (rāga):
"O Teacher of the World, may calamities befall me perpetually here and there."
"Your vision, which would be the vision of non-rebirth"—
that is, the seeing or beholding of You, who have become the object of action,
in those [verses].

The meaning is that it is "unprecedented" (*apūrva*) because its vision— whose perception of similarity has never arisen again elsewhere due to the absence of such sweetness anywhere else— is not born again.
// 1.8 // Śrī-Kuntī to the Blessed One // 89 // [90] She spoke out of affection: "Even though he is by her side or in private with her..."
Nevertheless, His pair of feet are ever-new at every step; for who could cease from His feet, since even Śrī, though she is fickle, never abandons them?
That Śrī Kṛṣṇa is situated by the side of those illustrious queens, remaining close to them; even there,
He stays in a secluded place, in private.
At every step, at every moment;
and this is not surprising for those who possess natural affection.
For who else indeed would cease from that state, being satisfied by the relish of that state?
In this regard, there is an illustration by way of a fortiori (kaimutya): "even one who is fickle," and so forth.
Although it is observed that in this world all things are by nature fickle,
here, for the purpose of strengthening the illustration,
there is an intention to express the non-difference between mundane and supramundane splendors.
// 1.11 // Śrī Sūta said: // 90 // [91] He spoke of the great state: "The gopīs experienced supreme bliss upon seeing Govinda."
For them, a single moment in his absence was like a hundred yugas.
This is clear.

This kind of affection consists merely of attachment; for among the devotees who possess knowledge, it cannot be the cause of excellence because the bliss of experience—being of the nature of a mass of supreme bliss—is free from the sense of "mine-ness.
This is likewise true even for those who are ordinary.
In passages such as "O Father, let there be for us existence in the hells through our own misdeeds" (BhP 3.15.49), however, this is merely a prayer for such passion on the part of Sanaka and others,
and not passion itself in its direct sense.
It should be concentrated upon;
however, in the case of those to be protected, it is limited to affection alone,
because possessiveness is clearly absent.
But it does not extend to affection and so forth, because that would be improper due to its remote connection; as for when...

In passages such as "O lotus-eyed one, you have departed" (BhP 1.11.9), and in the words of the citizens of Dvārakā— "there a single moment would be equal to ten million years"— the excellence of that [divine presence] is perceived. Indeed,
that is the state of feeling experienced by certain individuals there, such as barbers and florists, who were fortunate enough to enjoy direct service to Him.
It is connected as a statement possessing specific distinctions;
furthermore, even the culmination of passion toward the illustrious servants is possible due to their excessive sense of "mine-ness."
Because their very life consists solely in their constant and eager devotion to Him,

and because among those who are to be cherished, there is an even greater intensity of possessiveness due to the direct connection with the form of Śrī, one should understand that their passion is exceedingly intense.

Because their sense of "mine" (mamatā) toward those friends is even greater than toward their own parents—the foremost of whom are their affectionate father and mother—there is a superiority [of love] for them in every respect. Furthermore, as seen in Śrī Kuntī’s words, "May calamities befall me constantly elsewhere... (BhP 1.8.25), there is indeed a degree of excellence in their affection for their friends, though this superiority exists only in part. As for their well-wishers (suhṛtsu):
It is not from excessive proximity that there is an excess of love; rather,
affection and indignation occur only between a female friend and a beloved.
Now, among the beloveds of Śrī [Kṛṣṇa], this state culminates in the supreme *mahābhāva* of the illustrious principal queens (*paṭṭa-mahiṣīs*).
A particular transformation of this is the *vipralambha-śṛṅgāra* (erotic sentiment of separation) known as *prema-vaicitrya* (the wondrous variety of divine love).
This has been described by the passage beginning with "tāsām ūcur mukundaika-dhiyaḥ" (BhP 10.90.14) and ending with "ity īdṛśena bhāvena" (page 51);
beyond this, nothing more is heard.
But it is not heard that they have any attachment toward anyone other than those two;
indeed, this is the natural disposition of the virtuous who are filled with essential strength. [BhP 10.13.2]

In such passages and elsewhere, passion (*anurāga*) is described as manifesting a sense of novelty at every moment. However, passion does not have the mere manifestation of such novelty as its sole defining characteristic; rather, it consists of *ullāsa* (exaltation) and other such qualities.
Even though there is a momentary quality consisting of the manifestation of pleasure and pain, and the like, up to the limit of passion (*rati*) and other attributes,
in this case, because of the impossibility of the emergence of those respective characteristics in every instance, attachment is not determined; thus it is said,
"as in the case of the *navya*," and not "and not the *navya*."
For the illustrious queens of Vraja, however, there was the ultimate limit of *mahā-bhāva*;
those various nights were spent with their most beloved.
O dear one, by me alone, who remained within the range of Vṛndāvana,
those moments became like half a second; yet for them, being deprived of me, those same moments became equal to an entire kalpa.
This is because of such well-known statements as these;
and their inability to endure even a moment's blink is expressed thus:
"Your beautiful face with its curling locks of hair."
"Stupefied, they gazed at her, who made the eyes of onlookers tremble with their lashes" (BhP 10.31.15).

Regarding the passage beginning with "Whose face... (BhP 9.24.35), in the verse "The women and men were delighted, and Nimi was angry," the word *ca* indicates that, generally speaking, both the men and the women became joyful.
The meaning is that right there, some of the illustrious gopīs became angry with Nimi for blinking; this is because they had not heard of it elsewhere,
otherwise [they would have known] during the pilgrimage to Kurukṣetra.
And the cowherd girls, having finally found Kṛṣṇa— the long-desired object of their sight— cursed the eyelashes that obstructed their vision;
then, all of them, having embraced him who was already held within their hearts, were fully satisfied.
In the passage, "They attained that state which is difficult even for those constantly engaged in yoga to reach" (BhP 10.82.39),
there would also be the failure to achieve the intended distinction in the phrase "by the sight of whom," and so forth,
even though Śrī... [is present].
Although it is the very nature of Kṛṣṇa to generate such states of being, he nevertheless depends upon the qualities of the substratum,
just as water from the ocean depends on its source to produce pearls and the like;
and in this matter, they have attained that state.
The meaning is that they manifested a particular state of *mahābhāva* directed toward Śrī Kṛṣṇa;
for this very reason, it is said to be "difficult to attain even for those who are eternally united" (*nitya-yuja*).
Here, by the word *nitya-yuk*, those who possess that [state] are also implied.
Only those possessing the [required] characteristics are obtained as principal queens;
others who lack such characteristics are not, because they are too remote [in quality].

And thus, the meaning is that even those who consider themselves most beloved— thinking, "These women are separated from their lovers while we are constantly united with our dear ones day after day"— [acted as follows]: having heard this, Pṛthā, the daughter of Subala, and then Yājñasenī...
Then Mādhavī, the wives of the king, and her own cowherd women—
all of them, their eyes overwhelmed with a flood of tears— were greatly amazed at the continuous bond of affection toward Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Self and Hari.

In this context, the word *sva* (self) is used as a qualifier for the Śrī Gopīs— who, though astonished by the continuity of affection that touches upon the equality of their own internal state according to His previously mentioned manner in passages such as "Thus, in some other place not seen before, the women of Vraja desire..."— nevertheless, He acts through a mode of conduct never observed elsewhere.

For this very reason, even in the commentary on the verse *ataevāpitarāv upalabdhārtho viditvā* (BhP 10.45.1), the authors of the *ṭīkā* have established that their knowledge of His sovereignty was indeed already present;
however, the love arising from the state of being His sons is what is difficult to attain.
It has been stated that, in the same way, the status of the illustrious gopīs as one's own kinfolk is indicated in a general sense;
yet that [status] does not exist anywhere in Vraja, even in the case of the Vṛṣṇis, Kaṃsa, and others. (Page 58)
"When the people were wavering— everyone from children to the elderly and women, all behaving like beasts, O dear one, departed dejectedly from Gokula, longing for the sight of Kṛṣṇa," and so forth.
Because of this vision;

thus, since such is the case, a special distinction has arisen in the King of Cowherds himself, who possesses an invariably constant affection—so what need is there to mention that he is her child? This is the intended meaning.

// 10.43 // Śrī Śuka said: // 99 // [100] Thus, by virtue of having as their very nature the experience of the supreme excellence of sweetness, the state of being supremely wise is indeed accepted for the venerable Gopālas.
Therefore, even though the Brahman has manifested as infinite forms such as the four-armed one and others that have been seen, he has nonetheless taken their very form as his own object of support,
as expressed in passages such as: "I bow to You, the worshipful one, whose body is like a cloud" (BhP 10.14.1).
Furthermore, because it possesses that very intrinsic nature, this joy does not deviate from the knowledge of others which is adventitious; on the contrary,
it transcends that very [adventitious knowledge].

Therefore, it increases even when obstacles are imminent, just like the sensual pleasure of those addicted to sense objects. For even when the defects in sense objects have been heard of or seen by such people,
a powerful perception of their possessing qualities— attained through passion— is observed.

It has been stated in the same way: "That joy which belongs to those lacking discrimination" (ViP 1.20.19). And in this regard, there is the speech of the illustrious Nanda and Yaśodā addressed to Śrī Saṅkarṣaṇa:
"O descendant of Daśārha, Lord of the universe, protect us for a long time along with your younger brother!
Having thus placed him on their lap and embraced him, they bathed him with the waters of their tears. [BhP 10.65.3] And so forth;
by which [the people were made aware] that his status as the son of Vasudeva, his being a Kṣatriya, and his being the Supreme Lord had been manifested. Śrī...
The disposition of Baladeva as being fit for that [status of son] was not known otherwise;
as it was stated previously:
"O best of the Kurus, the Blessed Lord Balabhadra mounted the chariot."
Longing to see his friend, he set out for Nanda’s Gokula with great yearning.
"Embraced by the cowherds and cowherd women who had long yearned for him, Rāma saluted his parents and was greeted with their blessings. (BhP 10.65.1–2).
Thus, even for those whose nature consists of supreme sovereignty and knowledge, there occurs a temporary obscuration of those qualities through the intensity of affection.
This is observed, as in the case of the illustrious Devahūti: "When her husband had gone forth to the forest, she was distressed by the separation from her offspring;
though she had realized the ultimate truth, she became like a cow longing for her calf when it is lost" (BhP 3.33.21).
"I am terrified of Kaṃsa on account of you, O Śrī Devakī, for my mind is unsteady.
Thus spoke Śrī Yudhiṣṭhira:
"Ajātaśatru [Yudhiṣṭhira], for the protection of the army against the enemy of Madhu..."
Out of affection, yet apprehensive of others, he deployed his fourfold army.
And this was said for the sake of praising him:
"Then Śauri [approached] those who had come from afar..."
Having turned back the Kauravas— who were deeply affectionate toward him and distressed by their separation—
he departed for his own city with those dear to him.
Even in the statement thus spoken, because of such an intention;
likewise also for Śrī Saṅkarṣaṇa.
Having heard of this effort of the enemy kings and that Kṛṣṇa had gone alone to seize the maiden, the Blessed Rāma became apprehensive of a conflict.
Overwhelmed with brotherly affection, he went quickly to Kuṇḍina together with a great force consisting of elephants, horses, chariots, and infantry;
the meaning is that even though the Blessed One is omniscient.
Therefore, there is also the passage beginning with: "Then, seeing Kṛṣṇa seized by the great crane, Rāma and the other boys...
Thus, it being established that the knowledge of sweetness itself consists of powerful bliss, and in that regard, O Śrī...

Having transcended even the experience of being Brahman and Lord—which the cowherds had attained by their very nature—Śrī Śukadeva himself experienced a truly wonderful amazement through their good fortune, as stated in passages such as: "Thus, by the experience of the bliss of Brahman for the virtuous... (BhP 10.12.11).
In passages such as "Neither Viriñca nor Bhava [can grasp him]" (BhP 10.9.20),
and "He is not easily won" (BhP [referring to the passage concerning the son of the Gopikās]).
In this context, as in passages such as "He is not a limb of Śrī" (BhP 10.47.60),
and sometimes even when their nature is of that kind, the manifestation of their sovereignty serves to produce knowledge of sweetness by way of wonder.
Thus he nourishes [them]:
"How is it that this one, who is our son and so forth, can possess such actions?"
Thus:
"But Nanda and the others, seeing him, were filled with supreme bliss and tranquility; and they were greatly amazed to see Kṛṣṇa there being praised by the Vedic hymns," and so forth. [BhP 10.28.17]

Thus, because of their purity, the love of the girls of Śrī Gokula alone is most praiseworthy; as it was said: "Are you [the beloved] of these inhabitants of the cowherd settlement? (BhP 10.14.35)—even where [such love exists], it is found even among the animals.
Supreme affection is observed;
for example, when plunging into the Kālī lake,
the cows, bulls, and heifers cry out, being deeply distressed.
"With their eyes fixed upon Kṛṣṇa, they stood there terrified as if weeping" (BhP 10.16.11).

Likewise, "Upon his rising from there, the men, cows, bulls, and calves attained supreme joy" (BhP 10.17.16). Similarly, even among the stationary beings, having come together there, they found their desires fulfilled in Kṛṣṇa.
"Even the trees have withered" (BhP 10.17.65).
For this very reason, even the venerable Brahmā prayed:
"That birth in this forest is some kind of immense good fortune..."
"Even in Gokula, there is the bathing in the dust of His lotus feet.

Thus, since even in the glorious Gokula— the unique treasury of knowledge regarding supreme sweetness— His kinsmen are also included, He bears a particular sense of "mine-ness" (mamatā) toward both types of His beloveds.
For those of the lowest status, there is indeed a great exaltation;
as it was said: "Oh, what fortune! Oh, what fortune!
(BhP 10.14.32), and so forth. Herein lies the acceptance of the inhabitants of Vraja as friends by Him, even though they were the most lowly.
Thus, what is said indeed brings about only the praise of friendship. Now, he speaks of the excellence of friends even toward those [who are indifferent], saying:
"In this way, through the experience of the bliss of Brahman by the virtuous..."
Having become servants of the Supreme Deity,
those who had accumulated a multitude of merits sported together with the Son of Nanda, who was himself dependent on Māyā.
Manifesting as Brahman to the wise who are established in truth, he is rarely encountered; yet for those who have attained the state of servitude (dāsya),
for the liberated, and even for the perfected ones (siddhas), he is Nārāyaṇa, the supreme goal.

In accordance with the statement, "O Great Sage, one whose self is perfectly tranquil is extremely difficult to find even among ten million," that which manifests as the Supreme Deity is even rarer in its appearance than that,
for those who rely upon *māyā*.
However, for those devoid of knowledge, devotion, and friendliness, [the Self] does not manifest as the singular form of consciousness,
nor as the Supreme Lord, nor as the object of love.
Then, when his unique nature becomes manifest,
because there is no basis for [perceiving] his fitness [to be God],
the deluded despise me as one who has assumed a human body.
According to this principle, by means of the first three quarters of the verse, it is intended to show that His arising alone is difficult to obtain.
Consequently, with Śrī Kṛṣṇa— who is thus one whose manifestation is so hard to attain— one may indeed meet directly.
It is the wonder of Śrī Śukadeva that they lived even with their supreme friend [Nārada], who had ascended to the highest stage of love (*prema*).
Or rather, alas, at that time, by means of his all-pervading compassion, he [acted] toward those who have taken refuge in Māyā... [the commonality of]—

Even for ordinary people, he manifested a majesty that transcends all forms, appearing as the Supreme Brahman itself in human form; yet, despite such a gain being obtained from him, they did not attain the state of being his kinsmen. However, his friends attained with him an excellence of kinship that was of such a nature.

The meaning is that because they sported with Him as friends through their beauty, they alone have accumulated a multitude of meritorious deeds; thus, among the hosts who perform many virtuous acts to please the Blessed Lord, they are the most excellent.
For this very reason, such friendship does not exist even among other kinsmen, and thus their greatness has been established even over them.
Therefore, what need is there to describe the good fortune of these friends who sport with him in person, possessing a special inner affection characterized by intimacy? (Page 60)
As for those residents of Vraja who were commoners, let alone their other various fortunes,
even the mere sight of Him—
With the intention that even the fortune of other great sages is extremely difficult to attain,

one should support this very description of the friends' great good fortune by also explaining the subsequent verse: "The dust of whose feet [is attained] through the hardship of many births" (BhP 10.12.12).
For this very reason, Akrūra said at the verse beginning with "Then he descended" (BhP 10.38.15), "I bow to these two, and to our forest-dwelling friends.
Let that suffice for now; even though those friends and calves were taken away by Brahmā, [the Lord] created others.
Having seen those who were her equals, it occurred to her of its own accord;
yet, finding no satisfaction even with them, she brought those very friends— this too should be considered.

// 10.12 // Śrī Śuka said: // 100 // [101] Then, he spoke to them as well regarding his two venerable parents: "Therefore, let there be devotion toward Janārdana, who has become our son, the Blessed One."

"O Bhārata, the devotion of the couple toward the cowherds and cowherdesses was absolute," by which [verse] it is meant that their *bhakti* was *prema*, because it had ascended to the highest pinnacle of affectionate attachment. The cowherds...
All [the women] refers to the wives of the group of Gopīs who are His most beloved,
as required by what is to be said hereafter. Now,
because they are praised by the hosts of sages more than all others, their love, intimacy, pride, and passion are superior in every respect.

The majesty of those Śrī Vraja-devis who have brought Kṛṣṇa under their control through their own love—which uniquely possesses the perfection of *anurāga* and *mahābhāva* nourished by excellence—is indeed incomparable. It is precisely according to this sequence that the manner of Uddhava’s dismissal is observed, as follows: @- [Text continues...]

Then, having taken leave of the cowherd women, as well as Yaśodā and Nanda, and having bid farewell to the cowherds, the descendant of Daśārha, intending to depart, mounted his chariot. This is clear.
Therefore, having passed through all of Śrī-Gokula and seeing such states of physical and mental agitation among the gopīs due to their absorption in Kṛṣṇa,
Uddhava, filled with supreme joy, bowed down to them and sang this:
These cowherd girls on earth, who have fixed their love solely upon Govinda— the Self of all— are truly the supreme embodied beings;
for they desire that which the sages and even we ourselves long for out of fear of worldly existence.
What is the use of births as Brahmins for one who has tasted the nectar of infinite stories? Only those embodied beings who possess this supreme [devotion] have made their births fruitful;
therefore, [one should place] everything within the Self.
When Govinda— who is difficult for even all beings to perceive as the Supreme Self— manifests in their very presence,

shining forth directly as the Lord of Śrī Gokula, those whose states of being have taken root through the sweetness of such a particular emotion (*bhāva-viśeṣa*) become possessed of the Great Emotion (*mahā-bhāva*). This is precisely what occurred.

If the sweetness of that particular state of being— which is capable of reaching the ultimate goal of the intent of *mahābhāva*— should by chance come within the range of one's hearing through the medium of description,
then, having abandoned one's own nature...
Having reflected through the greatness of its manifestations that this state is the very pinnacle of love, we sages, desiring liberation from the fear of worldly existence, attain this—
just as these [goddesses] have done.
The meaning is that it lacks the capacity to experience the specific sweetness of that [nectar].
In this regard, he censures those who do not desire it: "In the narrations—indeed, in mere stories—of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, who is infinite and possesses infinite pastimes, what to speak of..."
For one who has no taste—meaning an absence of aesthetic flavor—for such stories, what is the use even of the Sāṅkhyas born from Viriñca?
The meaning is: nothing at all.
Now, it may be argued that they (the Sāṅkhyas) are indeed liberated or seekers of liberation, and are praised in the scriptures for their respective states; moreover, they are devotees.
But [this] is most excessive.
If that is so, how can there be a desire for those [women] elsewhere? To this he says:
"Where are these women wandering in the forest, corrupted by their infidelity?"
But where is this firm devotion to Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Self? Indeed,
the Lord directly bestows the highest good upon even the ignorant who worship Him, just as a sovereign medicine, when consumed, acts as a cure.
In that regard, because great devotion alone is clearly evident in those [sūtras] through the introduction, conclusion, and so forth of the illustrious Uddhava,
their deviation from the worship of Śrī Kṛṣṇa— and the fault inherent therein— is all the more apparent.
At the conclusion of the rāsa dance—
for all the embodied beings, both the gopīs and their husbands— (page 61).
He who moves within is the supervisor; through his play here, he becomes a possessor of a body.
Because this has been refuted by such passages as [BhP 10.33.35],
and because it is now being indicated that He Himself is indeed the Supreme Self; [this is so] according to the view of those of dull intellect.

Or rather, because their character of being prone to transgression is itself refuted by the very fact that the abandonment of what is to be attained is logically established in the verse, "But having abandoned the path of the noble ones" (BhP 10.47.61), it follows that the alternative meaning is irrelevant; thus, the meaning that is about to be stated is the only one that is consistent. As follows:
Regarding these women who wander the forest-dwellings of Vṛndāvana: with Kṛṣṇa as their refuge in that form, in what stage (bhūmikā) do they abide, or with respect to what [stage]?
By that [stage], such [women] are not corrupted by transgression.

Due to the absence of excellence in spiritual disposition (*bhāva*), there is a deviation characterized by a lack of intense attachment to that [state]; because of this defect, others such as those who fear worldly existence (*bhavabhī*) or ourselves—wherein we stand in relation to what stage (*bhūmikā*) therein?
Therefore, the sense is that there is indeed a vast difference.

How so? This one, whose devotion is fixed upon this Supreme Lord— who is seen here among these illustrious cowherd women and who is the object of longing for all as the most worshipful Supreme Self— has experienced the arising of the highest ecstatic emotion (mahā-bhāva).
It blossoms [only for them],
but not for us. Therefore,
the qualities of Śrī Kṛṣṇa— which produce such a state of being experienced by them— [are the cause].
"You are ignorant of the distinction; how then will you attain it even through the desire for it?
To this he replies with "nanu" (is it not so?), meaning "even for one who is ignorant."
The meaning here is that I myself, having been sent here unexpectedly, serve as the very illustration;
as it was said by her own self: "O highly fortunate one, [I have been separated] by separation."
"A great favor has been bestowed upon me" (BhP 10.47.27).
Alternatively, he confirms the aforementioned point by censuring even the great devoted wives who are averse to that rasa, asking, "Where are these women? (kvemāḥ).

Where are these women who sport in Śrī Vṛndāvana and are the beloveds of Śrī Kṛṣṇa? And where is that forest which is their forest of woodland pastimes (vanacaryās), by means of the elision of the letter 'a'?
They are distinct from those women who dwell [there],

yet they are women; for as stated in the description of the region of Ketumāla, according to the manner of Lakṣmī’s speech— beginning with "The vow-observing women [shall worship] you" (BhP 5.18.19)— they are [devoted] to the Supreme Self by their very nature.
Where are women who are corrupted by infidelity through turning away from Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the Lord of all? The sense is that there is a vast difference between them.
For in these [gopīs], He resides in the form of the crest-jewel of all human goals.
An established state is observed, yet there is not even a trace of it as there is in those [other women].
Thus, toward these women who possess supreme love, his affection would reach its highest degree;
for he says "nanu" (surely), because by his very nature he is a friend to all devotees.
What more need be said?
This is not a favor from Śrī, for she is devoted to those who take supreme delight in her; how much less so from other celestial women, who possess the fragrance and luster of lotuses?
On the occasion of the *rāsa* festival, from his arm-staff-like embrace of the necks of the beloved women of Vraja who had received his blessing, there arose upon his body—
that specific form of the glorious *śrī-vigraha* known as the Lord of Śrī-Vaikunṭha— the most beloved [consort].
Even for that intense delight and profound state of affection belonging to the beauty of Rūpā, there is no such manifestation of bliss as this grace;
if it does not exist even for Śrī, how much less for Nalina?

Even for those celestial women—the ladies of Vaikuṇṭha—who possess fragrance, beauty, and luster like that of a divine golden lotus found there, [such qualities] do not exist at all in others; how then could others have them? The meaning is that others are excluded even from afar.
To the question of how much clarity there is, as if in a cough, he says "rāsa" and so forth.
The meaning is that He is desirable even to Her, in accordance with the direction stated in the verse: "By the desire for whose form, the beautiful woman Śrī performed austerities" (BhP 10.16.36).

Therefore, this excellence of their state is not only evident in separation (*vipralambha*), but is also desirable even in union (*sambhoga*)—indeed, it is observable even in those who are [already] united. The implication is: "What then can be said of those like me?"

In the rāsa festival, for you who have attained your supreme desire by having your necks grasped with intense passion by the Lord’s staff-like arms—having received His blessing through that very embrace—the internal joy that had always risen within you, though previously concealed, has now reached full manifestation. And even that which... [api yat]... [is as follows].
In the passage from *BhP* 10.15.8, "spṛhā śrīḥ," which consists of words expressing rivalry with Lakṣmī,
the employment of the term "sundarīḥ" in the phrase "vraja-sundarīṇām" indicates that their beauty and other qualities are likewise [unrivaled].
He indicates that it is superior;

and this is logical because, according to the principle of Bhagavad-gītā 5.18.12, "He who has unalloyed devotion to the Blessed Lord," one attains excellence through the excellence of that [devotion].

Here, the gradation in both cases is shown solely by means of the "crown jewel of all states" (sarva-bhāva-śiromaṇi) and the "portion of the state of the beloved" (kānta-bhāvāṃśa), and not by means of the aspects of being born of devotion (bhakti-jāyatva) and being a wife (jāyātva), as in passages such as *na ca saṅkarṣaṇo na śrīḥ* (BhP 11.14.15).
Therefore, one should not consider it to be common to anything else;
it should be understood that because its object is the Supreme Lord Himself, characterized as Śrī Kṛṣṇa, it possesses a distinct excellence of its own. [105]
Therefore, let alone their desire to attain the splendor of existence;
rather, this alone is what I pray for— thus he said:
Oh, may I become even a shrub, a creeper, or a herb in Vṛndāvana that is graced by the dust of the feet of these women,
who have abandoned their own kin and the path of the noble for the sake of Him.
They took refuge in the state of Mukunda, which is sought after by the Vedas.

This is the meaning: for them, even the touch of the splendor of this particular love for Śrī Kṛṣṇa within me is not possible, because they possess the latent impressions (vāsanā) of births belonging to a different species.
And therefore, it goes without saying that there is no direct touch of their feet;
if that is so, then as for the touch of the dust of their feet—

"Among the portions of fortune consisting of the goddess Śrī, the shrubs, creepers, and medicinal herbs, may I become something or other of an unregarded form"— with these words, "Oh! she uttered, her heart pained by the longing [for such a state].
To the question "Of what sort [of women]?", he says: "Those who...

Indeed, those women who, because they are daughters-in-law of noble families, having abandoned their own kin and the path of the Aryas—which are difficult to renounce even upon superficial reflection—out of an excess of passion, [transgress] worldly and Vedic...
The meaning is "having transgressed the boundary.

In reality, however, [he has transgressed] such a supreme [reality], which is to be sought by the Vedas and determined— through the systematic reconciliation of all the Vedas— to be the crest-jewel of all supreme human goals.
Because the subject at hand is Mukunda in the form of the son of the King of Vraja, they have attained his path—the sequence of bliss resulting from union with him—which is characterized by *prema*.
The sense is that their notion, "Thus we abandon the path of the noble," is merely an illusion on their part. He who is that...
He himself reveals that the bliss of union is indeed extremely difficult to attain even for Śrī and the others;
for that which was honored by Śrī and by the likes of Brahmā, and even by the masters of yoga whose desires are fulfilled, within their own souls during the assembly of the *rāsa* dance—
Embracing that lotus-foot of the Blessed Lord Kṛṣṇa,
which had been placed upon their breasts, they abandoned their distress—
that very foot of the Blessed Śrī Kṛṣṇa who was resplendent in the assembly of the *rāsa* dance.
Having embraced that most excellent lotus-foot— which reveals the Lord's essence of sweetness and possesses an indescribable sweetness—
and which was placed [there] and offered by Him Himself, [he overcomes] his suffering.
They abandoned the mental anguish caused by not attaining Him directly;
yet even those masters of yoga, such as Śrī Śuka and others who were proficient in the yoga of devotion, worshiped Him within their own minds.

In accordance with the direction stated in the verse, "Desiring whom Śrī performed penance as a woman" (BhP 10.16.36), even Śrī has worshipped Him in her mind alone to attain Him; yet He has always been so from the beginningless past, and has never at any time been attained in person. That—
The sense is that it is because they have not been heard.

Thus, while his mind was fixed on paying direct homage to them alone, even as he was singing in such a manner, he again— due to being contracted by the weight of extreme wretchedness arising from the manifestation of his own great majesty— even there...

Considering himself unworthy, he bows to the dust of her feet; even there, out of humility, he pays homage specifically to the women of Vraja, as they share a common bond with that same circle, saying:
"I perpetually revere the dust of the feet of the women of Nanda’s Vraja."
"Their singing of the stories of Hari purifies the three worlds. With this second half-verse, I bow directly to the dust of the feet of such women as these; oh, how great is this for us! (page 63)
The sense is that even this fact—that they possess such fortune—is a great marvel. What is meant here is this:
"O beautiful lady, all these Yādavas are indeed my own attendants."
O Goddess, you are always dear to me, possessing qualities equal to my own.

Thus, according to the words of the Blessed Lord seen in the *Padma Purāṇa*, *Kārttika-māhātmya*— in accordance with such statements as "In sleeping, sitting, walking, and conversation" (*BhP* 10.90.46)— the Yādavas alone are indeed the most beloved of the Supreme Lord Śrī Kṛṣṇadeva. Therefore...
But those devoted to other manifestations remain far removed from [the ultimate truth] by their very nature.
As it is said: "Among other devotees, you are among the Yādavas, and I am among the Bhāgavatas" (BhP 11.16.29);
and "You are my servant, friend, and companion" (BhP 11.11.49).

According to the words of Śrī Kṛṣṇa spoken when He was subject to desire, such as "Uddhava is not even slightly inferior to Me" (BhP 3.4.31) and "Neither Saṅkarṣaṇa, nor Śrī, nor even My own self is equal to You" (BhP 11.14.15), [the Lord appears] through a portion of His devotion.
Uddhava alone is the most excellent in every respect;

yet his words of such humility are directed only toward the queens of Vraja, never even toward the principal wives [of Kṛṣṇa]. This very fact—that he has eyes only for their glory—is like the sight of one who was born blind.
The beauty of the full moon.

// 10.47 // Śrī-Uddhava // 102–107 // [108] Therein, they spoke of the greatness of the sixteen thousand wives of the illustrious Yadu-deva from among his own kin, as well as that of the eight principal queens.
Because she has reached the ultimate pinnacle, they said to the goddess Śrī Rādhikā:
"O virtuous lady, we do not desire sovereignty, nor self-rule, nor lordship over the earth;
nor even the status of Virāj, the position of Brahmā, or the infinite abode of Hari."
We desire to carry upon our heads the glorious foot-dust of this wielder of the mace, which is rich with the fragrance of the saffron from the breasts of Śrī.
The women of Vraja, the Pulindas, the grasses and creepers, and the cowherds all long for the touch of the feet of that Great Soul as He grazes the cows.
O virtuous lady, we do not desire sovereignty or other such things.

In this context, *sāmrājya* is the status of a universal monarch (*sārvabhauma*). *Svārājya* is the status of Indra. *Bhojya* is the state of being entitled to the enjoyment of both of those; it is derived from the root *bhuj* (to enjoy), meaning "one who enjoys," and the abstract noun formed from that.
*Virāṭ* means that which shines forth (*virājati*) in various ways;
its state (*bhāva*) is *vairājyam*. The meaning is the possession of the supernatural powers (*siddhi*) such as *aṇimā* and so forth. *Pārameṣṭhyam* refers to Brahman.

The state: according to the method of the Vedic revelation beginning with "Those hundred [blisses]" (TaittU 2.8.2), having demonstrated the ultimate limit of calculation for the bliss of Prajāpati by multiplying human bliss by a hundred times a hundred, [the scripture then states regarding the Supreme Brahman: "from which words turn back" (TaittU).
The meaning is: "even that" refers to the infinity of bliss shown by this [verse]. What more need be said?
We do not even desire that state of Hari, the Lord of Śrī, such as proximity and so forth;
the meaning is that we do not wish to make it dependent on us.

"In that case, what more do you desire? "No," they replied, "we merely wish to bear upon our heads the dust from the glorious feet of this wielder of the mace (Gadābhṛt), who is universally known as our husband."
We desire that;

even there, we desire all the more that which is enriched by the fragrance of the saffron from Śrī’s breasts—that fragrance by which a particular excellence of fortune is attained. This is the meaning.

Now, is it not the case that the foot of the Lord of Śrī alone is rich with the fragrance of auspicious saffron? [The Vṛtti here adds: "Because of its proximity, she came there; however, you have indeed abandoned it. And if Śrī were present here..."
If it is intended that [the fragrance] belongs to Rukmiṇī, then that has already been obtained by you;
