It has been established at the beginning of the *Bhagavatsandarbha* and so forth;
for this very reason, even though it is one, [it is so].
And of that power...
He states that [the Lord] is beyond *māyā* with the words: "in whom *māyā*, consisting of the three qualities (*traiguṇya*), has been destroyed by His own splendor and remains unmanifest.
This means that from whom *māyā*—the power whose nature is the three qualities (*traiguṇya*)—has been cast far away by His own essential power (*svarūpa-śakti*).
Therefore, it is utterly tranquil and free from all afflictions.
The reason for its being a mere manifestation of power is that it is other than the object of the inward-looking vision; it is not [an object thereof].
This is because of the Vedic revelation: "He sees forms with the eye" (KaṭhU 2.39), and "He is obtained by whomsoever He chooses; for him, He reveals His own form" (KaṭhU 1.2.23). Why is that?

"Name-and-form": these three deities, having entered by means of this living self (jīva-ātman), [thought], "Let us evolve name-and-form" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.3.2). It is thus devoid of the well-known, primordial name-and-form. The reason for this is stated as "inactive" (nirīha).

For by the word "Self" (ātman) in this Śruti, a portion of the Supreme Self in the form of the power called the individual soul (jīva) is denoted; [this is expressed] by the phrase "by this" (anena). (Page 100)
Because of the teaching of their distinctness,
"entry" in that form refers to the clinging to the limiting adjuncts characterized by fire, water, and earth, which are denoted by the word "deity."
And that [state] occurs for that individual soul (jīva) precisely because of the superimposition of "I-ness" (ahaṃtā) upon it;

consequently, although He Himself abides there in the form of the Inner Ruler (antaryāmī), due to the absence of such superimposition, He is devoid of the name and form produced by limiting adjuncts (upādhi).
The meaning is that this is indeed logical;
the intention is that when there is a complete absence of ego (ahaṅkāra), one is unfit for the application of the title "prophet" (vyākara-vāṇī). [195]

Now, [an objection is raised]: "Is it not the case that the form of Śrī Rāma is not perceived by everyone? To this he replies: "It is apprehended by the wise. The meaning is that it is perceived as one's own essential nature (*svarūpa*) by one whose mind is pure.
There is nothing higher than this, which is supreme.

This is known from the words of Śrī Brahmā beginning with, "Your true nature... [BhP 3.9.3]. Now, one might ask: what is the purpose of such a being appearing among mortals? It is said: when the primary [purpose] is already accomplished... [the secondary follows].
Furthermore, although there are other purposes, the primary one is indeed the manifestation of the sweetness of His pastimes among His devotees; thus He says:
"The descent of the Lord into the mortal world is for the instruction of mortals and for the slaying of demons, and not for any purpose alone."
Otherwise, how could there be calamities caused by Sītā for the Lord who delights in his own self? The word *tu* is intended to dispel such a doubt.
The descent, or manifestation, in the world of mortals does not serve merely to cause agitation and distress to virtuous people; rather, it also serves to instruct mortals.
Among mortals, that which consists of instruction and the illumination of its meaning is itself composed of that [devotion].
Within that, for those whose faces are turned outward, the manifestation of the inevitability of attachment to sense objects is incidental;
whereas the primary objective is one's own nature consisting of separation and union, which produces moisture in the heart within those whose mental impressions are fixed on devotion to oneself.
It is the manifestation of the sweetness of His particular pastimes;
therefore, the meaning is "for that purpose alone. Otherwise, if it were solely for the sake of His own destruction, then [He would not act] by virtue of being the Supreme Self.

For the Lord, who is complete, the inner controller of all, and who delights in His own essential nature and in Vaikuṇṭha— which is of that same singular nature— how could there be sufferings caused by Sītā?
It was [experienced] by the mind alone.
The sense is that because he is capable of killing and because such a calamity would otherwise be impossible,
those various things are indeed possible in the case of his manifesting his own sweetness. [196]
In this context, sweetness (*mādhurya*) consisting of compassion and such pastimes is especially praised.

Furthermore, it is shown that the sorrow of separation from Śrī Sītā is itself included within the sweetness of those pastimes, and thus there is no fault. Moreover, such pastimes are not like those of ordinary beings who are attached to lust and other worldly desires.
But he says that it is indeed by means of a particular compassion directed toward his own special kin:
"Truly, He is not the dearest friend of those who possess a self."
The Blessed Lord Vāsudeva is attached to the three worlds;
he would not succumb to dejection caused by a woman,
nor does he deserve to abandon Lakṣmaṇa.
He is indeed not attached to the three worlds; the reason for this is that he is the Self, the Supreme Self, the Blessed One.
Vāsudeva is the one who possesses perfect sovereignty and so forth, and is the refuge of all;
however, for those who possess a sense of "mine" regarding their own objects— those for whom He alone exists as their Lord, like a Self to those who have realized the Self.
The meaning is "of the particular devotees";
He is the dearest friend of those very people.
Therefore, unlike another...

Just as one experiences defilement caused by being female, he should not experience it [in that way]. Therefore, the meaning is that because she possesses a self (ātman), she is both the cause of such defilement and the object of his affection. Likewise, the abandonment of even the self-possessed Lakṣmaṇa, which occurred through the transgression of the agreement with the divine messenger—that indeed...
He says it is not absolute, meaning it is not a defining characteristic;
he does not deserve, nor is he able, even to abandon it.
Immediately thereafter, having ascended his own celestial chariot together with Sītā and others— who were waiting for his arrival while he was in heaven—
he is now likewise here with them.
(Page 101) Since we too are seen in the region of Kimpuruṣavarṣa,
the intention is that there is some imitation of this or that [custom] solely for the purpose of maintaining the boundaries [between regions]. [197]

In order to establish the very same point as before, he speaks with two verses on that supreme sweetness which is headed by compassion and has devotion as its sole cause, standing at the very pinnacle of all things:
"Surely there is no birth for one who is great, nor is there lack of good fortune..."
Neither speech, nor intellect, nor physical form is a cause for satisfaction;
for by these means, the elder brother of Lakṣmaṇa won the friendship of even the forest-dwellers who had been expelled from their homes.
The birth from the Great Puruṣa; good fortune, beauty, form, and caste— because of which [these qualities exist].

Alas! Even though we have been abandoned by Him due to those births and so forth, our elder brother—though He is marked by all the auspicious qualities of Lakṣmaṇa, the delight of Sumitrā, and though He is unsuitable for friendship or servitude—has nonetheless acted as a friend to us, being pleased by the devotion of His supreme devotee Śrī Sītā’s search for Him and other such acts. Together with him...
The meaning is that he made them like friends by means of providing dwellings and so forth; or rather, it was said thus with reference to Sugrīva.
Therefore,
whether he be a god, an asura, a monkey, or a human,
one who is supremely grateful for good deeds with all their heart—
"One should worship Rāma, Hari in human form,
who led the people of Kosala to the northern heaven. Thus,
by means of devotion consisting of knowledge of His true nature (*svarūpa-jñāna*), one should recognize that even in His human form He is the Supreme Reality itself.
He has shown this;
now, even through devotion consisting of the knowledge of sweetness, he especially worships that very Hari who possesses a human form.

There too, he distinguishes [the Lord] from Śrī Kapila and others by calling Him Rāma; He is supreme, possessing unsurpassed qualities, grateful for good deeds, and satisfied even with a very small amount of devotion.

// 5.19 // Śrī Hanumān // 193–198 // [199] Thus, in the passage beginning with “O Lord, you ought not to speak thus” (BhP 10.23.31), and also in the verse “You are indeed the dearest one, the friend, and the very self of all embodied beings” (BhP 10.29.32), she [the Goddess] expresses her inner intent through a paronomastic jest.
The manifestation of aesthetic flavor (rasollāsa) should be demonstrated foremost through the excellence of one's own internal emotion (bhāva).
Now, even through association with the secondary and the inappropriate, there is a manifestation of the primary; as in the case of skin, beard, body hair, nails, and hair—[BhP]
[10.60.45] Such are the words of Śrī Rukmiṇī.

Here, by way of *pratīpa* (contrariety), even that which is unsuitable— namely, the feeling of *bībhatsa* (disgust)— is connected [to the context], serving to praise the state of *kānta-bhāva* (the sentiment of the beloved) directed toward the subject at hand, Kṛṣṇa.
It was composed by means of a particular turn of phrase solely for the sake of its excellence;
therefore, it results in nothing other than the manifestation of aesthetic flavor (*rasa*).
Thus, it is said elsewhere:
Alas, these women perform deeds that are truly virtuous, having cast aside their natural feminine delicacy and abandoned all sense of purity—
those from whose home the lotus-eyed Lord departs as husband.
"Never departing, touching the heart with its allurements"—

here, "womanhood" (*strītva*) refers to the female species (*strī-jāti*), and that is understood in this context specifically through the distinctions of the lower classes within that species, such as Śrī Rukmiṇī and others.
It has been accepted that the rejection of qualities such as beauty and so forth refers to a different class [of women], and not to those such as Rukmiṇī and others,
because even by them, the virtue of those [other women] was established.

Furthermore, the meaning is that they purify even other classes of women who are possessed of various defects by means of their own fame and so forth; for when those [women] are adorned with all virtues free from such respective defects, then [the excellence of] those inferior to them [is established].
And he states the reason for establishing their excellence with the words "yāsām" (of whom).
Although he himself was of such a nature, [he was moved] by the utterances [of those women], which possess qualities appropriate for beloved ones. (Page 102)
— by means of these collections [of objects], which touch the heart and become attached to the mind, from whose home he never departs;
therefore, here too, there is the *bībhatsa* (the disgusting).
The term *saṅgati* (conjunction) is to be explained as before.
// 1.10 // "The women of the city of the Kaurava king" // 199 // [200] Now,

regarding secondary [meanings], even when there is a conjunction of primary meanings that are otherwise incompatible, there is an arousal of aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) according to the previous method, as for example:
The gopīs, their minds deeply attached to the infinite Lord,
remembering His friendship, smiles, glances, and words,
were tormented by intense grief when their beloved was swallowed by the serpent.
They beheld the three worlds as empty and bereft of their beloveds.

In this context, the appropriate rasa is indeed the secondary (gauṇa) karuṇa-rasa (the pathetic sentiment); therein, the *ujjvala* (brilliant) sentiment known as *saṃbhoga* (erotic union) is contrary to the situation.
Nevertheless, even there, the association with him— consisting of smiles, glances, and so forth—
is heightened by the mere fact of being remembered through the device of manifesting various emotional states;
thus, it results in the very emergence of rasa.

// 10.60 // Śrī Śuka // 200 // [201] Now, even when there was contact with those moving about among the principal [cowherds] who were unsuitable [for them], they were restrained by their husbands, as in the passage beginning: "Just as those [women] were being restrained by their husbands... (BhP 10.29.8).

And yet, in their presence, that very same fickleness— though otherwise improper— by way of manifesting an excess of delusion at that moment, led to nothing less than the heightening of the state of love (*kānta-bhāva*), known as *mahābhāva*, which is devoid of all other considerations.
"Therefore, the aesthetic flavor (rasa) truly shines forth," thus said Śrī Śuka.
Other examples should likewise be inferred in this manner.

Now, as for what was stated—that when there is an exaltation of an unworthy object, it is precisely the manifestation of *rasābhāsa* (the semblance of rasa)—an example of that is: "You two are not our sons; you are directly the Lords of Pradhāna and Puruṣa" (*BhP* 10.65.18).

In this case, devotion that has arisen by transgressing the parental affection (vātsalya) appropriate only for Śrī Vasudeva— who is manifested here in the role of a father— does not qualify as a rasa. And the resolution [to this objection] is as follows:
This should be applied according to the previous [explanation], just as in the case of Śrī Baladeva.
Furthermore, these reconciliations regarding the occurrence of a semblance of rasa (rasābhāsa) are made only with respect to those very instances that are free from defects.
But in other cases, that purpose is not supported;
therefore, the undesirable consequence must be avoided in every respect by means of what is appropriate.
Examples of the manifestation of aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) through association with worthy persons are to be inferred by oneself.
the flavors consisting of specific forms of that affection must be composed.
Therein lies the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) consisting of knowledge and devotion, which has "Peace" as its other name.
Therein, the objective basis (*ālambana*) is that which manifests as the Supreme Brahman through knowledge and devotion.
The object is the Śrī Bhagavān in forms such as the four-armed one,
as well as the great wise devotees engaged in the Lord's pastimes who serve as His support.

In that regard, the Lord himself was shown at that very time during the departure of Śrī Sanaka and the others for Vaikuṇṭha by such verses as, "The Lord whose navel is like a lotus" (BhP 3.15.27), and so forth; and the wise devotees and the sages who delight in the Self were shown by such verses as, "The wise devotees and the sages who delight in the Self" (BhP 1.7.10), and so forth.

These have been described; among them, it is indeed the *Śrī-Catuḥślokī* and others that are of such a nature. However, for Śrī Śukadeva, due to his being drawn by the sweetness of the nectar of divine play (*līlā-rasa*) and his intense devotion (*abhiniveśa*) to the *Śrīmad-Bhāgavata*, [he composed this].
One should be eager for that very [scripture] wherein the *Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam* is intended to be the supreme of all;
furthermore, its excitants (*uddīpanas*) consist primarily of qualities (*guṇa*), actions (*kriyā*), and substances (*dravya*). Among these, the qualities are: *sat*, *cit*...
The state of being intensely filled with bliss,
the constant attainment of one's true nature, and the state of being the Blessed One.
the state of being the supreme self, the predominance of the power of knowledge, and omnipresence.
The quality of bestowing liberation from enemies, and the quality of being dear to peaceful devotees.
equanimity, self-control, tranquility, and purity.
These include such qualities as possessing a wondrous form,
as well as activities such as protecting devotees,
and substances.
The dust from the feet of those who know the Mahopaniṣad and of the devotees, the tulasī, their sacred sites, and so forth;
furthermore, their spiritual potencies;
and the praise of their respective qualities and attributes, such as the Supreme Brahman and the Paramātman.

These include the utterance of the Name preceded by the disregard for the bliss of Brahman and the turning toward the Lord; as well as fixing the gaze on the tip of the nose, the gestures of an ascetic (avadhūta), the mudrās of knowledge,
yawning, stretching the limbs, bowing to Hari, offering praise, and so forth.
And those belonging to the sattva-guṇa are generally merely natural (prākṛta).
Now, the transitory emotions (sañcārin):
Disgust, fortitude, joy, intelligence, memory, despondency, longing, agitation,
discursive thought, and so forth; now, the permanent emotion (sthāyin) is knowledge and devotion (jñāna-bhakti), and that is—
You, who had vanished and remained hidden even within the hearts of the evil-minded,
have this very day been attained by us at the very roots of our eyes.
It is manifested by such verses as these;
and that which manifests the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) consisting of that [devotion] is described in that very same place:
The breeze, carrying the nectar of *tulasī* mixed with the filaments of the lotus-feet of that lotus-eyed one,
entered through their own openings and purified them.
It causes agitation even in the mind and body of those who abide in the Immutable.
And so forth.
Herein, the lotus-eyed Lord is the *ālambana* (the objective support),
and the wind is the *uddīpana* (the excitant).
The *anubhāva* consists of a specific manifestation in the form of physical agitation and a specific manifestation in the form of mental agitation.
Joy (*harṣa*) is the transitory emotion (*sañcārī*).
Knowledge-devotion (*jñāna-bhakti*), obtained through that specific designation by the phrase "even for those who delight in syllables," is the stable emotion (*sthāyī*).
It should be understood that aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) consists of knowledge and devotion, because it is established through the experience of their collection as a unity in one place.
Now, among the flavors consisting of devotion, the flavor consisting of the foundational devotion (*āśraya-bhakti*) is illustrated.

In this context, the *ālambana* (the objective support) is Śrī Kṛṣṇa, who manifests as the protector; the *āśraya* (the subjective locus) is the devotion (*bhakti*) directed toward Him; and the *dhārās* (the streams of emotion) are those belonging to the supreme objects of protection (*pālya*) involved in His pastimes.
Here, Śrī Kṛṣṇa—though appearing elsewhere primarily in a glorious human form—is essentially of the nature of the Supreme Lord (*parameśvara*).
And among the glorious residents of Vraja, however, there is indeed the supremely sweet and most powerful form of Śrī in the form of a human being.
Now, those to be protected by Him are of two kinds.
Those who are engaged in the activities of worldly manifestation are common and external [to the lineage],
while those whose very life is the shade of His feet are internal.
Among them, for the former, [the realization of] Brahman—
Śiva and others, however, are indeed internal to Him due to the presence of a particular excellence of devotion.
Furthermore, those in the northern region are of three kinds:
the common residents of Śrī Yadupura;
And there are the residents of the illustrious city of Vraja. Among them, in the first group, are King Jarāsandha’s captive kings and other such eminent sages;
the two subsequent groups consist of the guilds of people and so forth.
Now, regarding the qualities of the excitants (*uddīpana*): therein,
for those who take the form of the Supreme Lord as their object of focus, there is the state of being the Blessed One, the nature of being the seed for the descent of incarnations,
and the power of attracting even those who delight in the self (*ātmārāma*) by imitating His dress— even such beings as Pūtanā and others— through the state of being great devotees.

The state of being a giver of existence, the nature of the Supreme Self, the quality of having a single pore of the skin as the locus for infinite universes, and so forth— these, along with others to be described later, are mixed [attributes]. For those who assume the form of a glorious human being, there is the nature of an ocean of mercy, the protection of those who have taken refuge, and inconceivable greatness.
Power, supreme worthiness of worship, omniscience, firmness in vows, prosperity, a disposition of forbearance, courtesy, truthfulness, dexterity, the quality of making all things auspicious,
righteousness, the eye of scriptural wisdom, friendship toward devotees, generosity, vigor, and fame.
These include splendor, endurance, strength, submissiveness to love, and so forth; furthermore,

there are the "births" (jātayaḥ) of the former [Vaiṣṇavas], such as being a cowherd and the like, which are recognized through their imitation of those [divine qualities], as well as their reminders, such as their dark complexion and other traits.
Those two [categories] are understood as such solely by virtue of each subsequent one being superior;
now, [we shall discuss] the ritual actions.

For those who preceded [him], there were the acts of creation, maintenance, and so forth, as well as the manifestation of universal forms (*viśvarūpa*) and others to be described in the mixed [sections]. For those who followed, there was the refutation of opposing positions and the protection of one's own position.
These include his compassionate glances and so forth;
furthermore, there are the physical objects:
his weapons, musical instruments, ornaments, positions, footprints, artistic designs, and the like.
And those [powers] were clearly manifest to the former ones precisely because they were supramundane; whereas for the latter ones,
even though these very same powers are supramundane, their influence is displayed as if they were mundane.
Now, the times [are defined] as those connected to both his birth and his victory, and so forth.
Next are the secondary emotions (anubhāvas).
Through connection with them alone, there is the dwelling [in the heart], as well as the chanting of the names and qualities consisting of his power and other attributes.
[The first] and so forth; likewise those previously mentioned as well.
Now, the transitory [emotions]:
therein, in the context of yoga, joy, pride—
The *dhṛtis* (fortitudes). In [the state of] non-yoga (*ayoga*), there are fatigue and disease;
in both cases, there are despondency, apprehension, dejection, wretchedness, anxiety, memory, shame, pride, and so forth, as well as death.
That same [devotion] exists even in the context of yoga, as seen in the final life-story of Śrī Bhīṣma: "By means of pure concentration" (BhP 1.9.31),
and likewise in such passages as "Then, in that battle, the king of the earth [was struck] by my sharpened arrows" (BhP 1.9.34).
By the very phrase "as the skin was being torn apart," an example of dejection (*dainya*) expressed through words indicating one's own fault is to be illustrated;
this is also the case in passages such as "struck by the cold arrow" (BhP 1.9.38).
Now, the permanent [sentiment] is called the substratum-devotion (*āśraya-bhakti*); for example:
"O creator of the universe, may you be our existence;
you alone are our mother, our friend, and our father."
"You are our true guru and our supreme deity,
by following whom we have become perfected.
Here, even the *sāttvika* [emotions] and others are [manifested] solely through the distinctness of the *vibhāvas*, *anubhāvas*, and *udbhāsvara* [intensities].
Since it has been attained, one should also understand the illustration of rasa, which consists of the wonder arising from the convergence of those [factors].
As it has been said:
"If the true state [of rasa] should exist in the excitants (vibhāva) and so forth, whether in both or in one of them..."
"In that case, no fault exists because of the immediate implication (*samākṣepa*) of something else;
and this implication of something else occurs by virtue of the context. [SāhD 3.17] And so, the subjects of Dvārakā [addressed] the Blessed Lord: [204] [205]
The rasa consisting of devotion to the locus (āśraya-bhakti-maya) is of two kinds:
that characterized by non-union (ayogātmaka) and that characterized by union (yogātmaka).
Non-union is of two kinds: the initial failure to attain [the goal] and separation [from it].
And yoga is of two kinds: arising immediately after the two types of yoga in succession, namely, *siddhi* (accomplishment) and *tuṣṭi* (contentment).
Among these, the first is individual (*prātyātmikam*).
He states their lack of connection [to other teachers]:
"Thus, being obstructed by the Magadhas and longing for Your vision, they have sought refuge at the soles of Your feet; O Lord of the wretched, may welfare be bestowed upon them. [BhP 10.70.31]
Here, by the phrase "desiring a vision of the Blessed One," the desire for liberation from bondage is also indicated as being solely for the sake of that vision;
thus, the permanent emotion (*sthāyin*) is shown.
The root of the feet is the objective support (*ālambana*). Obstruction is the excitant (*uddīpana*) by way of opposition. Devotion is the radiant [excitant]. Longing is...
Dejection and agitation are the two transitory mental states (sañcāribhāvas).
From these, the sattvika and other [emotions] are to be understood.
// 10.60 // The royal messenger [approaches] the Blessed Lord. // 205 // [206]
Immediately following this, he describes for them the yoga known as *siddhi*,
beginning with: "They beheld him, dark as a rain cloud, clothed in yellow silk, marked with the Śrīvatsa, and possessing four arms" (BhP 10.73.2–3).
As if drinking with their eyes, as if licking with their tongues.
As if smelling with their nostrils and as if embracing with their arms,
those whose sins were destroyed bowed their heads at the feet of Hari.
With their exhaustion from confinement destroyed by the joy of beholding Kṛṣṇa,
the kings, with palms joined in reverence, praised Hṛṣīkeśa with these words.
In the phrase beginning with "pibantaḥ" (drinking), the word "iva" is used in the sense of poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*).
Because his eyes were wide open to the utmost degree from seeing that wondrous form, it is said that they were "as if drinking";
likewise, [they drank] his sweet...
Because of the longing to lick their lotus-feet, which had become fragrant, the yawns that occurred again and again are described as if they were licking those lotus-feet by means of that very sign;
for this reason, it is said they are "as if smelling" them.
Regarding the phrase "by means of the two nostrils":
by the sign of the expansion of the nostril-lobes, it is said that he seems to smell his entire body all at once.
The meaning is that its expansion was performed as if for that very purpose;
nevertheless, because of his devotion, it is appropriate that his desire be directed toward grasping the dust of his feet alone, and thus [it is so].
This has been explained;
the same applies to what follows.
By the sign of the movement of the arms produced by supreme possession (paramāveśa), that—
"Embracing, as it were, the lotus feet"— in every respect, the essential meaning is simply absorption in that. // 10.73 // Śrī Śuka // 206 // [207] Now, separation (viyoga).
In passages such as "When the lotus-eyed one departed" (*yarhy ambujākṣāpasasāra*), the power of the subjects of Śrī Dvārakā is made manifest;
and likewise, the Lord of the Yadus [is described] in relation to the subjects of Śrī Vraja.
In passages such as *dvirada-rāja-vihāraḥ* (BhP 10.35.25), the phrase *mocayan vraja-gavāṃ dina-tāpam* indicates that even for the cows,
calves, and children of Vraja who remained right there, [the heat was removed], let alone others.
The meaning is "of human beings.
Now, he describes the yoga called *tuṣṭi* (contentment), which arises immediately thereafter, for the subjects of Dvārakā:
Having approached his own prosperous kingdom of Ānarta, he blew his excellent conch shell,
as if to dispel the despondency of its people.
The word *iva* is used here as a poetic ornament (*vākyālaṅkāra*).
// 1.11 // Śrī-Sūta said:
// 207 // [208] This is made clear by the words beginning with "liberating even the subjects of Śrī-Vraja," and likewise by the forest of Vraja.
"Even for those who remain here, O friend, Vṛndāvana spreads the fame of the earth through the words of the Goddess of Vraja," and so forth;
"Alas, O women, listen to this wonder! (BhP 10.35.4).
It should be understood through these and other such [scriptural passages].
Now, regarding the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) consisting of the devotion of servitude (*dāsya-bhakti*):
therein, the *ālambana* (the foundational object) is the Lord manifesting as the master (*prabhu*).
Śrī Kṛṣṇa is the locus of devotion;
His support consists of His own exalted servants who are engaged in Śrī Kṛṣṇa’s pastimes.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa appears here in two forms: as the form of the Supreme Lord and as the glorious human form; these are indeed the manifestations previously described.
And His servants [appear] according to their respective inclinations.
They are of two kinds, and furthermore, those are of three types:

The passage beginning with *haro 'bhijātaḥ* (BhP 10.29.41) and ending with its conclusion consists of the words of Śrī Kṛṣṇa; herein, the first meaning refers to His request for union even when those women, though enchanted by His flute and other instruments, were acting with resistance.
The second, however, consists of rejecting their arrival for the sake of jest and to test their true intentions; likewise,
it consists of rejecting their entreaties even within their own words.
Therefore, because they consist of mutual and equal erudition, the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) is nourished to an extreme degree;

This is night;
if she has somehow arrived,

"You ought not to go;

Or else, they were the sons of co-wives and others.

By showing them his own pleasure grove, he inflamed their passion, as indicated by the verse, "The forest was seen" (BhP 10.29.21). He concludes with, "Therefore, go" (BhP 10.29.22), because this night is of a terrible nature.
The first is the cause;
therefore, let it not spread its sound for a long duration,

"Therefore, do not make them drink, and do not milk for that purpose.

"Having observed this as well, and that too, we shall become maidservants."

let alone talk of their breasts, do not place it even upon their heads.
Therefore, this being the case, the sense is: "Do not even mention such matters in your mind to women like me, who are born of noble families and are supremely chaste.
Thus ends the rejection of Śrī Kṛṣṇa’s request.

In that regard, relying on the science of knowledge (jñāna-śāstra) to refute that which has been established by the Blessed Lord— the permanence of following one's husband and others through the power of the instruction of the Dharma-scriptures— those women, by the mere movement of their own imagination, conceive of Him as the principle of the Supreme Self.

They establish that the intent of all instructions lies precisely in following Him, as stated in the verse beginning with *paty-apatya* (BhP 10.29.32). May this statement of instruction regarding one's own duty (*svadharma*) find its ultimate locus of intent in You alone, who are the goal of all such instructional statements.
The meaning is: "May it culminate solely in devotion to you. [An objection is raised: "How can I be the locus of that?
To this they reply: "You are the Self, the Supreme Self."
Therefore, by the force of such scriptural passages as "The Brahmins seek to know Him through the study of the Vedas" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.22),
the meaning is that you alone are the locus of that [Self].
Now, from what source is my status as the Supreme Self? To that, they say with insight:
"In common renown, You are the dearest of all embodied beings, the kinsman who is the object of unconditional love."
And you are one who acts for the benefit of others without any ulterior motive;

and these two qualities constitute the definition of the Supreme Self, according to the scripture of knowledge which begins: "But everything is dear for the sake of the Self" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.4.5).
This is well-established.
Therefore, it is proven that you alone are the Supreme Self.
Therefore, from you—

For us who were intent upon ritual worship, the Brāhmaṇa brought about detachment through the instruction of the scripture of more powerful knowledge, namely, "The uncreated is not attained by the created" (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 1.2.12), regarding our own duty (*svadharma*).
The sense is that there is no fault even in their renunciation.

It conveys that meaning, yet there is no intended emphasis (tātparya) upon it;
likewise, in this very manner, even through such spiritual instruction, they understood only Him (the individual soul) and not Brahman. [421]
Nevertheless, he expresses their longing for direct attainment [of Him], beginning with: "And they said, 'O Nalinanābha, Your lotus-feet... (BhP 10.82.48).
In this context, "O Nalinanābha," means:
Due to the intensity of our suffering, as we faint from the onset of longing for you, may your lotus feet arise even in our minds— those feet which, indeed,
according to what has been taught by you, are attained by those whose consciousness remains undisturbed.
"The masters of yoga should contemplate this in their hearts," and so forth; the commentary on the *Śrī-Kṛṣṇa-sandarbha* (KṛṣṇaS 170) should be consulted.
// 10.82 // Śrī Śuka // 414–421 // [422] Thus, the enjoyment (*sambhoga*) consisting of seeing, touching, and conversing has been shown here.
Furthermore, within that state characterized by dwelling together for three months, other specific excellences (*vaiśeṣya*) are also to be inferred. Now, moreover—
Even after the separation that arises immediately following that [union], the future *saṃbhoga* (enjoyment) which is characterized by non-interruption is also indicated therein;
for the Blessed One, having thus favored the gopīs, he—
Regarding the statement, "The Guru is the goal" (BhP 10.83.1),

and by saying "And they said," etc., it is shown that just as their desired end was the direct attainment of Him, so too, having been thus graced, He is to be attained as the Goal in His eternal state.

// 10.83 // Śrī Śuka // 422 // [423] In this very manner, it has been shown in the *Śrī Kṛṣṇa-sandarbha* according to the *Pādma Purāṇa*, Uttara-khaṇḍa, and other sources. For therein is described the return of Śrī Kṛṣṇa from Dvārakā to Vṛndāvana; at that time—
For two months, he sports with them because they are manifest in the world of manifold phenomena;
immediately thereafter,
because they are no longer manifest, he grants them eternal union.
In the eleventh [chapter] as well, that very same point was clearly stated by Him Himself to Uddhava:
"There, together with Rāma, [He went] to Mathurā..."
In the two verses beginning with "praṇīta" (BhP 11.12.10), it is said that those women, whose intense longing was for union, saw no one other than Me as a source of happiness;
thus, those various nights spent separated from Me became like kalpas. (BhP)
By this past-tense usage, it is indicated that at that time there was no separation;
immediately thereafter, the joy of the splendor of attaining Him is described.
They were unaware of their attachment to me.

By the two verses beginning with *baddha-dhiyaḥ* (BhP 11.12.12), it is shown that those whose minds are bound by the attachment following the great separation (*mahā-viraha*)— being true devotees— experience something indescribable at that time through the immersion in supreme bliss.
They did not perceive [anything else]; the meaning is that they attained joy and delusion.
In this regard, there is an illustration for their knowledge being solely intent upon Kṛṣṇa, beginning with "as if" (yathā).
There is also another meaning for this.

In the *Śrī-kṛṣṇa-sandarbha*, regarding the verse beginning with "Desirous of Me, they took him as their lover" (*mat-kāmā ramaṇaṃ jāram*) [BhP 11.12.13], he describes in the immediately following verse how they perceived him; this has been explained there both in detail and in brief.

They attained Me, known as Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Brahman; yet, being unaware of His true nature as their own eternal beloved, they had previously attained Him in the form of a lover. Nevertheless, they were such that their desire for Me was characterized by the longing for Me as their husband.
"But the form of the lover comes later.
From this, it is explained that their appearance as belonging to another is due solely to their consisting of a few moments.
This very point is intended in the *Ujjvala-nīlamaṇi* of our venerable predecessors, upon whom we depend.
Regarding that introduction:
"That [love] is not desired by poets when it belongs to another's wife;
therefore, this [love] is for the sake of the family of those with lotus-eyes from Gokula."
"By the Enemy of Kaṃsa, the crest-jewel of the circle of connoisseurs, these [works] were brought down out of a desire for the aesthetic flavor (rasa).
Since such a conclusion regarding the activity is made at the very moment of the descent [of the scriptures], [the work is established as authoritative].

And in the conclusion of the *Lalitā-Mādhava* (7.18), in the passage beginning with "Alas, she who bears a body that has been burnt," there occurs the fulfillment of the fruit known as *samṛddhimat* (the enriched) within the subsequent pastime following the removal of the delusion regarding her status as a paramour.

Because enjoyment (*sambhoga*) has been demonstrated, one should understand that there are other intermediate subdivisions of this fourfold enjoyment— which is nourished by the four types of deception and consists of the triad beginning with manifestation— as follows, for example, through play (*līlā*).

These include stealing, singing together, the *rāsa* dance, water-sports, wandering in Vṛndāvana, and so forth. Among these, the pastime of stealing is as follows: "Having taken their garments, he quickly climbed a *nīpa* tree," and so on (BhP 10.22.9). This is clear.
// 10.22 // Śrī Śuka said:
// 423 // [424] "There was a certain gathering together with Mukunda," and so forth; likewise:
"Then, at one time, Govinda and Rāma of wondrous prowess..."

They spent the night in the forest, moving in the midst of the women of Vraja, while being gracefully sung to by those women who were bound by deep affection; their limbs were well-adorned and anointed, they wore garlands, and they were dressed in spotless garments. (BhP 10.34.20–21), and so forth.

This is generally the occasion for the *horikā* festival; for even while he was with his brothers, he enjoyed diversion with women in Vraja itself, according to the injunctions of the *Bhaviṣyottara*.
Even today, the custom of the people of Āryāvarta is seen to be exactly like that; and here, they honor the onset of night when the moon and stars have risen. [BhP]

Thus, due to that delusion, on the full moon day of Phālguna— which is possessed of its own splendor at the end of the frosty mists of the Hemanta and Śiśira seasons and when the moon and other luminaries shine— their radiance is described.
Therefore, at that time—
Union with Śrī Rāma, who possesses the joy of friendship, is indeed appropriate;
however, the reading "in the forest at night" occurs only in certain [manuscripts].

And in that context, the forest should be understood as being situated within the cow-pen (*vrajāntastha*). Śrī Śuka says: "There Govinda began the *rāsa*-pastime with his devoted followers" (BhP 10.33.2), and so forth. This refers to the *rāsa*. [425–427] The *rāsa*. There Govinda began the *rāsa*-pastime with his devoted followers... and so on.
Water-sports: "He was thoroughly drenched with water by young women... and so forth.
Strolling in Vṛndāvana: "And then, in Kṛṣṇa’s grove, where the quarters of the horizon were filled with breezes scented by the flowers of the water and land... and so forth. This is clear.

// 10.33 // He // 425-427 // [428] Now, as for *samprayoga* (union), it is as in: "the stretching out of arms, the embrace, the formidable thighs, and the knot of the lower garment" [BhP 10.29.46], and so forth; this is clear.

// 10.29 // He // 428 // [429] Furthermore, this radiant pastime (*līlā*) of Śrī Kṛṣṇacandra related to the *rāsa* dance is also considered to be infinite— as in the verse beginning with "Thus, the nights illuminated by the rays of the moon" (BhP 10.33.25). Now...
They describe the pastimes of Śrī Rādhikā, who possesses all auspicious fortune and whose crest-jewel is turned upward: "Whose feet are these, belonging to her who has gone with the son of Nanda?"
Like a female elephant whose forearm rests upon the shoulder of her mate.
Surely the Blessed Lord Hari, the Sovereign, has been propitiated by her,
since Govinda, being pleased, has left us and led her into a private place.
Oh, blessed indeed are these particles of dust from the lotus feet of Govinda,
which Brahmā, Śiva, and the goddess Ramā bear upon their heads for the destruction of their sins!
These high positions of hers cause us great agitation,
since she alone, having carried off the Gopīs, enjoys the lips of Acyuta in secret.
Surely her footprints are not visible here because of the young grass shoots;
her beloved lifted up his beloved, whose well-formed soles were being pained by them.
"Look, O cowherd women, at these steps of Kṛṣṇa, the lover, as he carries his bride while overcome by the weight of her burden."
There, the beloved was planted by the Great-Souled One for the sake of flowers;
here, the gathering of blossoms was performed by the Beloved for the sake of his dear one.
As he gazed at these footprints where the entire soles were visible,
he saw that the lover had here performed the decoration of his beloved's hair; those locks, surely, had been arranged in a topknot as she sat down upon him.
In this context, "whose" refers to all [the women];
"by her" refers to the friends;
and "blessed" refers to those standing on the bank.
"Of her" refers to the remedies (*pratipakṣa*). "They are not perceived" refers to the friends who are causing her distress. "These" refers to the remedies that cannot endure that [distress].
In this context, "planted" (*avaropita*) is used together with the friends; "hair" (*keśa*) is used again with half of the adversaries;
and "those" (*tāni*) is used again with the friends.
This is to be understood; for by employing various words referring to that couple, their mutual affection and other qualities are manifested.
As it is said: "But those who were distressed upon seeing them spoke thus" (BhP 10.30.26).
The suffering of all [beings] has been described; that too is certainly applicable everywhere through one's own particular longing.
// 10.30 // The Goddesses of Śrī-Vraja // 429 //
In that regard, within the pastimes of that Sovereign of Śrī Vṛndāvana, the two verses beginning with "eṇapatnī" (BhP 10.30.11), although previously shown, should also be contemplated.
In this regard, whatever commentary was not expanded upon for fear of prolixity should be consulted in the *Śrī-daśama-ṭippaṇī* by those desiring to experience the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*).
Thus, by this passage, the purpose of the treatise has been explained;
and let it be so.
Protected by the gopīs, blossoming forth, gazed upon with joy,
and everywhere made fragrant with delight in the production of flowers and fruits;
he shines sweetly in the land of Vṛndāvana with a splendor that surpasses all.
May this wish-fulfilling tree of joy bring delight to me through Rādhā and Mādhava.
Victorious is Kṛṣṇa, the embodiment of pure consciousness, who has descended here to manifest such a state of being, and who is the refuge for the multitude of wicked people.

Thus ends the *Śrī Bhāgavata-sandarbha*, which contains the essence of the teachings of Śrī Rūpa and Sanātana— who were disciples of the feet of the Lord Śrī Śrī Bhagavat Kṛṣṇa Caitanya Deva (who descended for the purpose of purifying the Kali-yuga and distributing His own worship)— and who were the recipients of honor from the assembly of all the kings of Vaiṣṇavas.
The sixth compendium, named Prītisandarbha.
In this *Śrī-Bhāgavata-Sandarbha*, which contains all the *sandarbhas* within its womb,
the sixth *sandarbha*, named *Prīti*, has here reached its conclusion in a fitting manner.
This sixth compendium is concluded.
This work is complete:
the Śrī-Prīti-sandarbha.
